items.title: Nana Konadu Yiadom I: A letter to my fellow Queen Mothers II
items.description: Nananom, my sisters. I write this letter not as someone standing outside our institution looking in, but as one of us. I write as a woman freshly enstooled and still learning what this office asks of me. I write with humility to my senior sisters, whose service across decades has shaped what I am now inheriting and whose example forms the ground on which every younger queen mother stands. I write because I believe we owe each other a conversation that our public appearances rarely permit, and because the moment we are living in will not wait for us to have it later. The clothes are beautiful. The ceremonies are meaningful. The appellations carry history. The respect our communities give us is an inheritance generations before us preserved at great cost. None of this is small, and none of it should be treated as small. But none of it, by itself, is the work. And the work is what I want to write to you about. I want to ask a question, and I want us to sit with it honestly. What is a Queen Mother for? Not what she should wear. Not where she should sit at a durbar. Not who should rise when she enters a room. What is she for? What becomes better because there is an Ohemaa in the community? Which girl remains in school because her queen mother intervened? Which struggling mother finds help because her queen mother organized the women around her? Which widow is protected? Which young person finds direction? Which injustice becomes impossible to ignore because an Ohemaa stood up and said, enough? These are uncomfortable questions. I believe we must ask them anyway. The stool was not entrusted to us merely to give us status. It was entrusted to us so that we could give service. What We Actually Inherited Long before development agencies began speaking the language of “women’s empowerment,” African women were already exercising authority within sophisticated systems of family, lineage, commerce, diplomacy, community organization, and traditional governance. Our foremothers advised. They negotiated. They organized. They protected women and children. They traded. They resolved disputes. They preserved lineage and identity. They served as diplomats and, when history demanded it, defenders of their nations. Our inheritance, therefore, is not one of silence. It is one of responsibility. Our elders have long said that a wise child honours the mind of her forebears. To honour our foremothers is not only to remember what they did. It is to carry the same seriousness into the work that is now ours. Within Asante tradition, the developmental role of traditional leadership has taken on renewed importance in the modern era. Under the reign of His Majesty Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, Asantehene, development-oriented traditional leadership has become an increasingly visible part of the work of stools and communities throughout Asanteman. For those of us who serve as Nkosuohemaa, the title itself carries the language of development. It tells us something. It tells us that leadership in this century cannot rest only on ceremony. It must also address the social and economic advancement of our people. The stool I now occupy has therefore caused me to think deeply about what traditional authority must mean in a modern community. We remember Nana Yaa Asantewaa because when history placed a demand on her leadership in 1900, she did not retreat into ceremony. But Nana Yaa Asantewaa should not become so monumental in our memory that we miss the ordinary lesson her life leaves for leadership. The lesson is not that every queen mother must lead a war. The lesson is that the stool must mean something when the community needs us. There is a danger in remembering powerful women only as historical figures. We praise them at anniversaries. We print their faces on banners. We tell their stories to schoolchildren. But history becomes comfortable when we admire courage without allowing it to make demands on our own lives. It is easy to celebrate Nana Yaa Asantewaa. The harder question is what courage looks like on my stool today, and on yours. It is worth remembering that the tradition we inherit is not only historical. It is still being written. In our own time, a Cape Coast woman named Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang has become the first female Vice President in the history of our republic — the first woman to lead a state university in Ghana as Vice-Chancellor before that, a former Minister for Education who spent her portfolio fighting for the girl child, an advocate whose voice on child marriage, domestic violence, and sexual abuse has shaped a generation of policy in this country. She stands at Golden Jubilee House because Ghanaian women have never accepted that leadership is not their inheritance. If she can carry that authority into the second-highest office of the republic, none of us on our respective stools has any excuse for accepting a smaller version of the leadership our own communities are asking of us. For one queen mother, courage may mean confronting parents who intend to remove a gifted girl from school. For another, it may mean challenging a practice that continues to harm women simply because it has existed for generations. For another, it may mean demanding accountability for community resources. For another, it may mean gathering unemployed young people and refusing to accept that idleness is their destiny. And for another, it may mean walking into a government office, a university, a bank, a foundation, or a business and asking plainly for the partnership her community needs. Courage does not always arrive with a war drum. Sometimes it arrives with a school register, a meeting agenda, a funding proposal, a hospital referral, a scholarship list, or a difficult conversation that everyone else has been avoiding. The Comfort of Ceremony I want to ask this next question with respect, because I include myself in it. Have some of us become too comfortable with the ceremonial version of our office? We attend funerals. We attend durbars. We receive invitations. We sit in places of honour. We wear the cloth. We are introduced by our titles. Each of these has its proper place. Ceremony carries culture. Protocol preserves order. Tradition gives a people continuity. But ceremony cannot become the destination of leadership. Our people cannot eat protocol. A brilliant girl cannot pay her school fees with our title. A young man without work cannot build a future from our photograph at a durbar. A pregnant woman frightened to attend a clinic does not need only our blessing. She may need our intervention. At some point, leadership must become visible in people’s lives. That is why I believe our generation of queen mothers faces a choice. We can inherit the stool as an ornament of history. Or we can inherit it as an instrument of change. I know which inheritance I want. Why Trust Is Our Economic Power There is a specific reason the queen mother’s stool matters to development, and I do not think we have fully appreciated it. That reason is trust. An economy is not made only of markets, banks, and money. It is also built on relationships between people who believe that others will honour their word. Where trust is weak, everything becomes harder. People hesitate to cooperate. Credit becomes more difficult. Projects collapse after disagreements. Communities struggle to mobilize around shared priorities. Trust, therefore, is not a sentimental thing. It has economic value. And the queen mother’s stool often carries something that governments, businesses, and development organizations spend years trying to build community trust. When an Ohemaa convenes women and they come, that is an asset. When market women, farmers, professionals, and diaspora members respond because they trust the institution she represents, that is an asset. When a respected woman can encourage parents to allow their daughters to attend training, can organize women around savings, can bring professionals into a community, or can persuade people to contribute toward a shared project, something economically significant is happening. This is what I have come to think of as development capital. A queen mother may possess several forms of it at once. She may have legitimacy capital because the stool carries cultural authority. She may have trust capital because the community believes in the institution. She may have network capital through professionals, institutions, businesses, and the diaspora. And she may have mobilization capital because she can bring people together around a purpose. These are not decorative assets. Properly organized, they can become development power. This is why the developmental question is not simply whether queen mothers should participate in economic and social development. The deeper question is whether we are prepared to use — deliberately, responsibly, and at scale — the trust our communities have already placed in us. The Stool Is a Public Trust Since becoming Nkosuohemaa of Kwabre Abirem in April 2026, one conviction has settled heavily on me. I did not sit on the stool to be admired. I sat on the stool to work. And I suspect many of my sisters feel the same calling, whether or not they have found the words for it yet. Across Ghana, queen mothers are already doing important work, often quietly and with limited support. They help children remain in school. They settle family disputes. They organize women. They support the sick and vulnerable. They advocate for girls. They raise funds. They mentor young people. They connect communities with professionals at home and abroad. Much of this never reaches a newspaper. That is precisely why this letter is not a condemnation of queen mothers. It is an invitation to recognize the scale of what becomes possible when we become more intentional about the authority we already hold. The strength of a queen mother, however, should never depend only on her personal energy. Strong leaders build structures. Our women’s councils must become working councils — with women of experience in education, health, finance, business, and community mobilization, with professionals from our towns who live elsewhere in Ghana and abroad given meaningful ways to serve, with basic records, annual priorities, assigned responsibility, and honest follow-up. This does not require expensive bureaucracy. It requires seriousness. The difference between an institution and a personality is whether the work continues when the person is absent. If a queen mother’s entire development agenda exists only in her head, the stool has not yet built an institution. Our goal must be to leave behind structures stronger than the ones we inherited. The Work Is Shared None of what I am describing is work a queen mother can or should do alone. And none of it should be undertaken outside the wider traditional order. Our chiefs, elders, and traditional councils are partners in whose company this work must proceed. The queen mother’s stool has always existed in relationship with the chief’s stool. When I speak of queen mothers stepping more fully into development leadership, I do not speak of competition with our chiefs. I speak of partnership. Traditional governance is strongest when authority is exercised with mutual respect, consultation, and clarity of purpose. Any Nkosuohemaa who mistakes development leadership for a contest with the male traditional order will accomplish less, not more. The goal is not to weaken traditional authority. The goal is to make the whole institution more responsive to the needs of the people it serves. Our Girls Are Watching There is another reason this conversation matters. The girls are watching. Somewhere in every community is a girl who is learning what female leadership looks like by studying the women who already possess authority. She may never become a queen mother. That is not the point. She is watching whether a woman with authority is expected to speak. Whether she is expected to think. Whether she can lead. Whether she can disagree respectfully. Whether she can manage resources. Whether she can sit with chiefs, ministers, businesspeople, and professionals without shrinking. Whether she can challenge injustice. Whether she can organize. Whether she can dream beyond herself. Every time a queen mother uses her authority wisely, a girl learns something about the possibilities of womanhood. Every time we reduce ourselves to ornament, she learns something too. Our communities are not only listening to what we say. They are studying what we normalize. Three Questions from Every Stool I am not calling for every queen mother in Ghana to follow the same programme. That would misunderstand the beauty of our communities. Every stool has its own needs. One town may need sanitation. Another may need maternal-health support. Another may need youth employment. Another may need help for market women. Another may need to mobilize its diaspora. The priorities will differ, as they should. But I believe every queen mother should be able to answer three questions about her stool. What does my community need most? What authority, relationships, and resources does my stool possess? What am I going to do with them? That is where development begins. Not with a title. With a decision. If you have not already done so, convene your women’s council before the next festival and put three measurable priorities on paper. Not twenty. Three. Name who is responsible for each. Set a date by which the first visible result must be achieved. Begin there. The movement I am describing in this letter does not begin with a conference. It begins with a meeting. A Word to Our Sisters Across the Water Much of what I have written applies also to those reading from London, Toronto, New York, Washington, Amsterdam, and the many other places where Ghanaian women have built lives and careers. Distance does not erase responsibility. Our professional training, networks, experience, and capacity to organize can become powerful assets to our hometowns. Diaspora women can mentor girls. They can help schools. They can connect entrepreneurs to markets. They can support scholarship funds. They can introduce hospitals, universities, and nonprofit organizations to communities that would otherwise never reach them. They can bring expertise as well as money. If you are a professional woman with roots in a Ghanaian town, your queen mother may be one of the most important calls you make this year. Introduce yourself. Ask what is needed. Offer what you genuinely can. And if you are a queen mother with people from your town living abroad, do not wait for them to guess what the community needs. Organize them. Give them something credible to support. Give them accountability. Give them a reason to believe that their contribution will become visible work. The distance between Chelmsford and Kwabre Abirem is smaller than it looks when there is real work to be done. A Quiet Movement Is Possible I have found myself imagining, more than once, what might happen if queen mothers across Ghana decided collectively, but without waiting for anyone’s permission, to redefine what active traditional female leadership looks like in this century. Imagine thousands of queen mothers each choosing three measurable priorities and holding themselves accountable to them. Education registers in traditional areas. Women’s savings groups linked to credible financial institutions. Health campaigns organized through palaces. Mentorship networks connecting girls to professionals. Scholarship funds. Enterprise training. Diaspora committees with real work to do. Imagine queen mothers exchanging practical ideas across regions — an Asante Ohemaa learning from a Ga Manye, a Dagomba women’s leader sharing a maternal-health model with sisters elsewhere, an Ewe Mamaga exchanging community-enterprise ideas with queen mothers in Fante or Nzema. Imagine the knowledge already sitting inside our traditional systems moving horizontally across Ghana, community to community, woman to woman. Not every solution needs to begin in a ministry. Some solutions already exist in our communities. They simply need to travel. This does not require a revolution against tradition. It would be a movement through tradition. Quiet. Practical. Local. Woman-led. And difficult to stop once communities begin seeing results. Conclusion There comes a moment in every generation when an inherited institution must decide whether it will live only through memory or live again through action. I believe that moment has come for us. Our foremothers have already demonstrated that African women can lead. We do not need to prove that again. The question before us is what we will do with the authority now resting in our hands. Years from now, our stools will pass to other women. They will wear the cloth. They will hear our names. They will inherit whatever institutions we leave behind, or whatever silence we leave in place of them. What will they say about us? Will they say we preserved the ceremonies? I hope so. Will they say we respected our elders and protected the dignity of our traditions? I hope so. But I hope they will be able to say more. I hope they will say that these were the queen mothers who kept girls in school, who organized women economically, who brought professionals and the diaspora home to build, who protected vulnerable children, who strengthened families, who formed partnerships, who understood that a stool without service is only decoration. I hope they will say that these were the queen mothers who worked. Nananom, the stool already gives us a platform. Our communities give us trust. Our histories give us legitimacy. Our relationships give us reach. What remains is what we choose to do with them. So, I return to the question with which I began. What is a queen mother for? Each of us must answer it from her own stool, in her own community, in her own generation. But I know this much. We were not enstooled merely to sit. We were enstooled to stand when our people need us. To speak when something must be said. To organize when something must be built. To protect when someone is vulnerable. To challenge when complacency has settled in. To serve. And to leave the stool stronger than we found it. Nana Yaa Asantewaa stood at Ejisu in 1900 and fought the war. What she preserved was something the empire could not carry away: the demonstration that when the political order breaks, the women can hold. One hundred and twenty-six years later, a daughter of Cape Coast stands at Golden Jubilee House as Vice President of the republic, proof that what Nana Yaa Asantewaa preserved has never left us. The line runs unbroken from her stool to ours. The question is whether, in our own time, we too will hold. My sisters, let us stand. Nana Konadu Yiadom I is the Nkosuohemaa of Kwabre Abirem in the Ashanti Region. Professionally known as Barbara Acheampong, MBA, EA, NTPI-F, she is a Tax Resolution Strategist, PhD candidate, and Board Chair of the Otumfuo Foundation USA. This is the second piece in her series on the queen mother’s stool as an instrument of transformation.

items.title: Burkina/Fiscalité : 143 conseils fiscaux admis à l'inscription au tableau de l'Ordre prêtent serment
items.description: Une année après l'adoption de la loi portant sa création, l'Ordre national des conseils fiscaux du Burkina Faso (ONCF-BF) enregistre les premiers inscrits au tableau de l'Ordre. L'acte a été porté par une cérémonie solennelle de prestation de serment qui a eu lieu dans la matinée de ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026 devant le Tribunal de grande instance Ouaga I. C'est la première cohorte donc de conseils fiscaux inscrits à ce premier tableau de l'Ordre national des conseils fiscaux du Burkina Faso (ONCF-BF). Cette inscription fait suite à l'adoption en juin 2025 par l'Assemblée législative du peuple d'une loi réglementant la profession de conseil fiscal au Burkina et ce, après une quinzaine d'années d'attente par les acteurs du secteur. Ce sont au total 143 personnes qui sont inscrites à ce tableau de l'Ordre des conseils fiscaux du Burkina Faso (trois étaient absentes à la cérémonie de prestation de serment). C'est dans une forte mobilisation de parents, amis et autres proches que s'est tenue la cérémonie, articulée essentiellement autour de la lecture des actes y afférents, du réquisitoire du Parquet, puis de la prestation de serment à proprement parler avec chacun de ces spécialistes présents dans cette salle d'audience. « C'est avec un grand plaisir, un grand bonheur, que nous éprouvons ce moment. Nous recommandons donc à ces personnes qui viennent de prêter serment d'observer scrupuleusement les prescriptions légales qui encadrent notre profession. (…). Nous exercions dans un environnement où il n'y avait aucune loi qui encadrait la profession, n'importe qui s'improvisait conseil fiscal. La bataille pour arriver à un Ordre n'a pas commencé aujourd'hui, c'est une lutte qui a démarré depuis les années 2010 et nous y sommes arrivés en 2025 », a, à l'issue de la cérémonie, exprimé le président de l'Ordre, Adama Bitié, insistant sur l'importance de la prestation de serment pour la profession, l'État et le contribuable. Ici, en interview, le président de l'Ordre, Adama Bitié (milieu), encadré de proches collaborateurs. Le premier responsable de l'organisation, M. Bitié, a donc saisi l'instant pour inviter les nouveaux assermentés à s'approprier les exigences de la loi et à faire en sorte que la profession puisse servir pleinement sa vocation. Pour rappel, selon l'article 3 de cette loi portant règlementation de la profession de conseil fiscal et création de l'Ordre national des conseils fiscaux au Burkina Faso, est conseil fiscal toute personne physique ou morale, habilitée conformément aux dispositions de la présente loi, qui exerce à titre habituel une activité d'accompagnement des contribuables dans le domaine de la fiscalité. Les missions du conseil fiscal sont l'information et la sensibilisation des contribuables sur la législation fiscale ; la consultation et le conseil en matière de fiscalité ; l'assistance dans l'établissement et la déclaration des obligations fiscales ; l'assistance ou la représentation devant l'administration fiscale, les juridictions ou autres instances compétentes conformément à la règlementation en vigueur. Dr Amadé Bagaya. Le conseil fiscal a également pour missions l'audit fiscal, la révision ou l'expertise judiciaire dans les conditions prévues par la loi. Il peut, par ailleurs, assurer les missions de conseil juridique d'entreprise ; analyser la situation et le fonctionnement des entreprises et organisations sous leurs aspects économiques, juridiques, financiers et informatiques ; assurer tout mandat d'accréditation conformément aux textes en vigueur. Ramata Sangaré Pour les nouveaux assermentés, Francis Neya, Ramata Sangaré et Dr Amadé Bagaya, la prestation de serment est également « un engagement et une interpellation à plus de rigueur dans l'exercice de la profession ». Elle est aussi, peut-on retenir, gage d'assurance pour le contribuable, qui sait désormais qu'un Ordre (voir composition du bureau au bas de la page : Ndlr) régule l'exercice de la profession de conseil fiscal et qu'il peut, en cas de besoin, y recourir pour ses besoins d'accompagnement ou pour toute autre préoccupation liée au secteur. Francis Neya Lire aussi : Burkina / Adoption d'une loi réglementant la profession de conseil fiscal : « C'est un challenge pour les futurs membres de l'ordre national des conseils fiscaux », estime Dr Amadou N. items.title: Enta Fassa : sommés de quitter les lieux, les vendeurs de bétail réclament un délai
items.description: L’avenir des vendeurs de bétail du site d’Enta Fassa reste incertain. Sommés de quitter les lieux, ces commerçants souhaitent obtenir un délai avant tout déguerpissement. Ce mercredi 25 novembre, notre rédaction s’est rendue sur le site afin de recueillir leurs préoccupations et de comprendre les raisons de leur opposition à un départ immédiat. Sur place, l’inquiétude est palpable. Les vendeurs affirment vivre dans la peur depuis plusieurs semaines et passer désormais leurs nuits sur leur lieu de travail pour protéger leurs animaux et les investissements consentis dans leur activité. Selon leurs témoignages, une opération menée aux environs de 4 heures du matin, la veille, par des agents de la CMIS 4 d’Enta aurait conduit à l’interpellation de plus de 20 personnes. Ces dernières auraient été retenues jusqu’à 14 heures avant d’être libérées. Ils affirment par ailleurs être en règle avec les services des impôts, disposer des documents administratifs nécessaires à l’exercice de leurs activités et avoir fourni des détails aux autorités communales. « Actuellement, nous passons la nuit ici parce que nous avons peur. Nous avons des milliers, voire des millions investis dans les béliers et les moutons. Cela fait près d'un mois que nous dormons ici chaque jour pour surveiller nos animaux. Hier encore, à 4 heures du matin, le maire est venu avec la CMIS 4 d'Enta. Ils ont interpellé plus de 20 personnes. Nos téléphones et nos clés de moto ont été retirés. Nous avons été conduits dans leurs locaux où nous sommes restés de 4 heures à 14 heures », témoigne l’un des représentants des vendeurs. Il poursuit en expliquant que la mobilisation de certains de leurs collègues, qui ne passaient pas la nuit sur le site, a finalement permis d’alerter les médias. « Nos amis qui étaient chez eux ont fait appel aux médias. Lorsque le colonel et le maire ont vu les images à la télévision, ils ont finalement décidé de nous libérer et de nous restituer nos affaires. Il y a également eu des échauffourées entre les vendeurs et les agents de la CMIS 4. Certains ont reçu des coups. Nous avons aussi enregistré des pertes au niveau du bétail : six chèvres et un mouton sont décédés », raconte-t-il. Au-delà de cet épisode, la principale préoccupation des commerçants reste la menace de déguerpissement. Ils affirment ne pas vouloir entrer en confrontation avec les autorités, mais souhaitent obtenir un délai supplémentaire pour continuer leurs activités. Le représentant des vendeurs insiste notamment sur leur volonté de respecter les décisions des autorités communales, tout en demandant au maire de tenir compte de leur situation. « On ne peut jamais être en désaccord avec le maire puisque c'est notre chef. Mais nous lui demandons toujours de nous laisser ici pendant un bon bout de temps. Après l'aménagement du site de Sonfonia, nous irons là-bas. Le ministre de l'Élevage travaille déjà sur ce projet depuis longtemps et nous sommes derrière lui », affirme-t-il. Pour justifier leur demande, les vendeurs évoquent les difficultés liées aux différents espaces qui leur auraient été proposés. Ils citent notamment un premier site situé à Dabompa, qu’ils jugent inadapté à leurs activités. « Le maire nous a déjà montré plus de deux sites. Il y a d'abord celui de Dabompa, mais ce site est vraiment inadapté pour nous. Il est rempli de boue et le bétail ne peut pas être installé dans de telles conditions. Le deuxième site se trouve au niveau du rail. Vous savez qu'on ne peut pas vendre du bétail sur les rails. C'est dangereux pour les animaux, mais aussi pour nous-mêmes. Nous ne voulons pas être en confrontation avec l'État. Nous demandons simplement au maire de nous laisser ici encore quelque temps », explique-t-il. Les commerçants affirment toutefois être favorables au projet de transfert vers Sonfonia, annoncé par le ministère de l’Élevage. Ils disent être disposés à rejoindre ce nouvel espace dès que les travaux d’aménagement seront achevés et que les conditions nécessaires à l’exercice de leurs activités seront réunies. Le représentant des vendeurs évoque également un autre argument pour contester l’urgence de leur départ. Selon lui, un terrain situé à Limania aurait déjà été identifié dans le cadre d’un projet de construction d’une boucherie moderne. « On nous menace de déguerpissement en nous faisant croire qu'il existe ici un projet de l'État concernant l'implantation d'une boucherie moderne. Pourtant, nous savons que le ministère de l'Élevage, en collaboration avec le maire, a déjà identifié un site à Limania pour ce projet. Cela est connu de tous », soutient-il. Autre point sur lequel ces commerçants tiennent à insister : leur situation administrative et fiscale. Ils rejettent toute idée selon laquelle ils exerceraient leurs activités en marge des obligations légales. À l’appui de leurs déclarations, ils présentent des quittances et différents documents qu’ils disent avoir obtenus auprès des services compétents. « Nous sommes conformes à la loi ici. Nous sommes installés depuis 1996. Le fondateur de ce site l'a créé cette année-là. Cela fait donc plus de 30 ans que nous sommes ici. Nous avons les documents de l'État. Nous payons les impôts, nous payons la salubrité et nous disposons de toutes les pièces nécessaires pour exercer nos activités. Voici les quittances et les documents que nous présentons », affirme-t-il. Pour ces vendeurs, un départ précipité pourrait avoir de lourdes conséquences sociales et économiques. Ils rappellent que plusieurs générations ont exercé sur ce site et que de nombreuses familles dépendent directement de cette activité pour leur subsistance. « Ici, il n'y a pas que des personnes qui n'ont pas été à l'école. Nous avons des élèves, des étudiants, des diplômés et des pères de famille qui ont cinq ou dix enfants à charge. Nous avons également des veuves. Tous nos revenus viennent de cette activité. Si nous perdons cet espace, une partie de la population risque de se retrouver dans la précarité », alerte le représentant. Face à cette situation, les commerçants lancent un appel au président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, afin qu’une solution soit trouvée à leur situation. « Aujourd'hui, nous avons peur. Nous sommes tellement effrayés parce que nous savons que l'État est le plus fort. Mais nous sommes aussi dans nos droits et nous sommes des citoyens guinéens. Nous demandons humblement au président de la République, Son Excellence Mamadi Doumbouya, de nous venir en aide. Nous ne refusons pas de partir. Nous demandons seulement un délai raisonnable pour ne pas perdre tout ce que nous avons construit ici », plaide-t-il. Tout en réaffirmant leur adhésion au projet de transfert vers Sonfonia, les vendeurs souhaitent donc pouvoir poursuivre leurs activités à Enta Fassa jusqu’à ce que le nouveau site soit véritablement opérationnel. En attendant une réponse des autorités, ces commerçants restent dans l’expectative, entre la crainte de perdre leur espace de travail et l’espoir d’une issue favorable à leurs doléances. Christine Finda Kamano L’article Enta Fassa : sommés de quitter les lieux, les vendeurs de bétail réclament un délai est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: ‘I’m done with Rivers, FCT; give me Imo, Kwara to deliver’ – Wike tells Tinubu
items.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has asked President Bola Tinubu and the Director General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, to assign him Imo and Kwara states, saying he has completed his political mobilisation work in Rivers State and the Federal Capital Territory. Wike made the request during a town hall meeting with residents and members of the Rainbow Coalition in Gokana Local Government Area of Rivers State. The minister said he had been assigned to coordinate Rivers and the FCT but was now seeking two additional states to work on ahead of the next election. “I was assigned to coordinate Rivers State and the FCT. Frankly speaking, I am done with these states, and we have no work to do again,” he said. Wike said he wanted the President and the campaign director general to give him more responsibilities, adding that he was willing to take charge of Imo State because of what he described as political challenges in the state. “As I am going now, I will plead with the Campaign DG and President Tinubu to add two more states for me to deliver. It’s a serious matter,” he said. He also referred to reports of divisions within the political structure in Kwara State, saying he would like to take responsibility for delivering the state for Tinubu. “From what I am told, they are having some problems in Imo State. So, I will like to go there and deliver Imo for Mr President,” Wike said. “Secondly, I have not confirmed, but what I read on social media is that there are some divisions in Kwara. So, I plead with the DG of the APC Presidential Council, Senator Yari, and Mr President to allow me to take over Imo and Kwara States, because I am done with Rivers and FCT,” he added. Wike’s remarks signal his willingness to take on a wider political mobilisation role in support of Tinubu, although he acknowledged that his information about the alleged divisions in Kwara was based on social media reports and had not been independently confirmed. items.title: Les ambassadrices et cheffes de mission au Sénégal appellent à une réponse collective
items.description: À l’occasion du lancement des 16 Jours d’activisme contre les violences faites aux femmes et aux filles, des ambassadrices et cheffes de mission au Sénégal alertent sur l’ampleur des violences facilitées par les technologies. Elles plaident pour une meilleure protection des victimes, un accès effectif à la justice et la fin de l’impunité des auteurs. Les violences faites aux femmes ne s’arrêtent pas aux portes du monde numérique. Cyberharcèlement, traque numérique, diffusion d’images intimes sans consentement ou encore contenus truqués (deepfakes) constituent autant de formes de violences auxquelles les femmes et les filles sont de plus en plus exposées. Face à cette réalité, des ambassadrices et cheffes de mission au Sénégal appellent à une mobilisation collective pour faire de l’espace numérique un environnement plus sûr. Dans une déclaration commune des ambassadrices de plusieurs pays, notamment la Finlande, la Belgique, l'Irlande, l'Union européenne, les Pays-Bas, le Venezuela, le Luxembourg, la Suisse, le Portugal, l'Espagne, le Royaume-Uni, le Pakistan, le Canada et la Suède, ainsi que par des responsables du système des Nations unies et d'organisations internationales au Sénégal publiée à l’occasion de la campagne des 16 Jours d’activisme, prévue du 25 novembre au 10 décembre, les signataires rappellent que le thème de cette année, « Tous unis pour mettre fin à la violence à l’égard des femmes et des filles : garantir la justice, protéger les survivantes et mettre fin à l’impunité », trouve un écho particulier dans l’univers numérique. Elles soulignent que les violences en ligne ont des conséquences bien réelles sur les victimes. « Chaque message de haine, chaque image volée, chaque menace reçue sur un téléphone atteint une femme ou une jeune fille qui a peur, qui se tait, parfois qui s’efface », alertent-elles. Une situation qui peut également exposer les victimes à des conséquences difficiles à maîtriser. L’ampleur du phénomène est préoccupante. Selon les chiffres d’ONU Femmes, basés sur une étude de l’Economist Intelligence Unit, 38 % des femmes dans le monde ont déjà subi des violences en ligne. Pour les signataires, ces agressions représentent autant de vies, de carrières et de voix mises en danger. Une responsabilité partagée Pour les ambassadrices et cheffes de mission, la solution ne saurait consister à demander aux femmes de quitter les réseaux sociaux pour échapper aux agressions. « Leur demander de se retirer des réseaux serait une double peine : subir la violence et perdre leur espace de liberté », préviennent-elles. Elles estiment que la lutte contre ce phénomène exige une réponse concertée impliquant les États, les plateformes numériques, les médias, la société civile et les familles. Les États doivent notamment garantir l’accès à la justice, tandis que les plateformes sont appelées à intégrer la sécurité des utilisatrices dès la conception de leurs outils. Les signataires insistent également sur la nécessité d’associer les jeunes femmes aux réflexions et aux décisions concernant les technologies. « Elles sont des actrices du changement, pas seulement des victimes à protéger », soutiennent-elles, estimant que leur expérience du numérique doit davantage peser dans la conception des outils et les politiques qui façonnent les technologies de demain. Trois engagements pour protéger les victimes Dans leur déclaration, les diplomates et responsables d'organisations internationales formulent trois exigences prioritaires. La première concerne la garantie de la justice, à travers des mécanismes de signalement simples, la préservation des preuves numériques et des recours effectifs pour les victimes. Elles préconisent également un travail sur la diffusion et l'efficacité des dispositifs de signalement existants. Le deuxième engagement porte sur la protection des survivantes. Il s'agit notamment d'assurer le retrait rapide des contenus préjudiciables et de renforcer l'accompagnement juridique et psychosocial, en développant des réponses conçues avec les jeunes femmes. Enfin, elles appellent à mettre un terme à l'impunité. « Auteurs sanctionnés, plateformes tenues de rendre des comptes », résument-elles, insistant sur la nécessité d'une responsabilisation de tous les acteurs concernés. À travers cet appel commun, les signataires rappellent que les droits des femmes ne connaissent pas de frontières entre les espaces physiques et virtuels. « Nous, Femmes ambassadrices et Cheffes de mission au Sénégal, nous tenons aux côtés de chaque femme et de chaque jeune fille : leurs droits ne s’arrêtent pas à l’écran », affirment-elles. Leur ambition est de contribuer à bâtir un environnement numérique dans lequel chaque femme et chaque jeune fille puisse s'exprimer librement, participer à la vie publique et influencer les transformations technologiques sans craindre les violences. A.N

items.title: Kogi govt hails Tinubu for paying N25m campaign signage fee
items.description: Kogi State government has commended President Bola Tinubu for paying the prescribed N25 million levy for outdoor campaign advertisements in the state, ahead of the 2027 general elections. The Commissioner for Information and Communications, Kingsley Femi Fanwo, who disclosed this to newsmen in Lokoja yesterday, described the President’s action as a demonstration of respect for the rule of law and equality before the law. He noted that compliance by political leaders would encourage other candidates and political parties to fulfill their obligations. Fanwo said the President had demonstrated that the law applied equally to everyone, regardless of political position, influence or status. “The President has once again demonstrated his belief in equality before the law. When the President of the country complies with a state law, it sends a strong message that nobody is above the law. We commend him for this example and urge other political actors to follow suit,” he said. The Commissioner explained that the government had substantially reduced the approved campaign signage fees following a series of consultations and stakeholders’ meetings with political parties and other relevant interests. According to him, the reductions were made after listening to stakeholders and reaching a common ground that would make payment more convenient and affordable for political parties and candidates. “We did not just wake up and impose fees on political parties and candidates. We held several meetings and consultations with stakeholders. We listened to their concerns, considered their submissions and agreed on adjustments that would make compliance easier. “For instance, the presidential campaign signage fee was reduced from N150 million to N25 million. The senatorial fee came down from N50 million to N20 million, while that of the House of Representatives was reduced from N30 million to N10 million. For the House of Assembly, the fee was reduced from N5 million to N1.5 million. “These reductions were deliberate. We wanted to make payment convenient and ensure that the fees were affordable. The agency did its part by listening to the political parties and making reasonable concessions. We now expect everyone to do their part by complying with the law,” Fanwo stated. The Commissioner further clarified that the Signage and Advertisement Law covered a wider range of political campaign materials beyond billboards and posters. He explained that branded vehicles, campaign shirts, fez caps and other branded promotional materials used for political campaigns also fell within the scope of the law and attracted the applicable levies. “The law is not limited to billboards and posters. It also covers branded vehicles, branded shirts, fez caps and other campaign materials used for outdoor political advertising. Anyone using these materials for campaign promotion must understand that there are legal requirements to fulfill. “We cannot allow people to exploit gaps in public understanding to evade their responsibilities. The law is clear, and the agency will continue to educate stakeholders while ensuring that everyone complies,” he said. Fanwo warned that the government would henceforth move beyond the removal of illegal billboards and campaign posters to prosecuting individuals and organisations that violate the law. “Enforcement is not only about pulling down billboards and removing posters of defaulters. We will prosecute them henceforth. It is a law, and it is binding on all political parties and all candidates. Once you engage in outdoor political advertising without paying the required levy, you have violated the law and will be held accountable,” he warned. He stressed that the government would not allow political considerations to undermine the enforcement of the law, adding that signage revenue remained an important component of the state’s internally generated revenue. “Signage is one of the critical revenue-generating areas of government. The revenue is important for the delivery of public services and the development of our state. We cannot allow political activities to become an excuse for revenue leakages. The law must be respected, and everyone must play by the same rules,” he added. The Commissioner also commended Governor Usman Ododo for ensuring that the implementation of the law remained free from political interference. “We thank His Excellency, Governor Ahmed Usman Ododo, for providing the leadership that has made this possible. He has ensured that the Agency is allowed to do its work without political interference. This is important because the credibility of any law depends on its fair and consistent application,” Fanwo said. He called on all political parties, candidates, campaign organisations and advertising practitioners to obtain the necessary approvals and pay the prescribed levies before mounting campaign billboards, posters or deploying other forms of outdoor political advertising. Fanwo maintained that the government would continue to engage stakeholders while insisting on compliance, adding that the law would be enforced fairly and without discrimination. items.title: Police confirm shooting as Obi, NDC hold town hall in Edo
items.description: By Ozioruva Aliu BENIN CITY — The Edo State Police Command has confirmed a shooting incident involving supporters of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) who gathered to welcome the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, to Benin City, leaving one person injured. The incident occurred along Airport Road as NDC supporters lined the route to welcome Obi and his entourage to the state capital for a town hall meeting. The suspects, said to be three in number, reportedly arrived at the scene in a black Toyota Hilux vehicle before opening fire on people gathered in the area. Confirming the incident, the Police Public Relations Officer of the Edo State Command, Eno Ikoedem, said the assailants opened fire after encountering police operatives stationed at the airport exit gate. “Upon sighting police operatives stationed at the Airport exit gate, the assailants, unable to proceed, made a U-turn and opened fire on persons at the scene before fleeing,” she said. Ikoedem identified the injured person as Aimionkhale Michael, who sustained gunshot wounds to his thighs and was rushed to hospital for medical attention. She said the Commissioner of Police, CP Patrick Daaor, visited the scene and subsequently went to the hospital to assess the victim’s condition. According to her, additional police personnel were deployed to the town hall venue and the hospital to prevent further attacks, while tactical operatives were mobilised to track down the fleeing suspects. The police spokesperson said the Commissioner had directed the Deputy Commissioner of Police in charge of the State Criminal Investigation Department to conduct a thorough investigation in collaboration with eyewitnesses and ensure that those responsible were brought to justice. The command condemned the attack and warned individuals and groups against actions capable of threatening public safety or disrupting the peace of the state, particularly as political activities intensify ahead of the 2027 general elections. It urged residents to remain calm, continue their lawful activities and provide credible information that could assist the investigation. The command assured residents that measures were being taken to apprehend the suspects, adding that it would not tolerate attempts by criminal elements to undermine security in the state. APC chieftain denies involvement Meanwhile, an APC chieftain, Eriyo Osakpanmwan, has denied allegations linking him to the shooting incident. In a viral video recorded at the scene, a voice was heard alleging that the Toyota Hilux used in the attack belonged to Osakpanmwan. However, when contacted, the APC chieftain dismissed the allegation, saying he was with the Edo State Governor, Monday Okpebholo, campaigning in different parts of the state at the time. “We have been campaigning everywhere with the governor and today I have been with the governor campaigning and we just finished the campaign for today. “How can I be with the governor campaigning and I will also be accused of being involved in any shooting incident? It is strange to me,” he said. The post Police confirm shooting as Obi, NDC hold town hall in Edo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghanaian award-winning artiste M Jay set to release single ‘Ngolo Kante’
items.description: Ghanaian award-winning artiste M Jay is preparing to release a new single, ‘Ngolo Kante!’, a motivational Afrobeat-dancehall record built around perseverance, self-belief and staying focused in the face of doubt. The announcement follows a strong run at the Ghana Music Awards Europe 2026, where M Jay was named Best Diaspora Hiplife-Pop Artist of the Year and Best Diaspora New Artiste of the Year. Speaking to YFM Ghana, the musician explained that the song grew out of his own journey as an artiste. Musicians, he noted, regularly face criticism, setbacks and moments when people question their vision. ‘Ngolo Kante’ is his answer to that: keep working, stay focused and keep pushing forward regardless of what others think. The title borrows from the French footballer N’Golo Kanté, whose career is widely admired for its resilience, discipline and consistency. M Jay says those same qualities have helped him keep chasing his goals, and he wants the song to carry that spirit. Asked how the project differs from his earlier releases, M Jay described it as a more mature version of himself as an artiste. He said he experimented with new sounds and different songwriting approaches, and went deeper into storytelling. The project, he added, reflects both his artistic growth and his willingness to step outside his comfort zone. He was also more intentional about telling his story and expressing the mindset that has kept him motivated through difficult times. Listeners can expect themes of perseverance, self-belief, hard work and overcoming obstacles. According to M Jay, the song speaks to anyone who has been doubted, underestimated or challenged while chasing their dreams. At its core, he said, it is about staying true to yourself and trusting the process, even when the journey is not easy. Musically, M Jay hopes to showcase his growth and introduce a sound that connects Afrobeat and Afrodancehall in a unique way. Career-wise, he hopes the single will reach new audiences, create more opportunities and help people discover his music and story. “I want listeners to leave feeling motivated and confident,” M Jay said. No matter the challenges they face or what people say about them, he wants them to keep moving forward. “If this song inspires even one person to believe in themselves and keep pushing, then I’ve achieved my goal.” In short, ‘Ngolo Kante’is a motivational Afrobeat-dancehall anthem about resilience, self-belief and staying focused on your goals despite criticism and obstacles. Inspired by M Jay’s own journey as a musician, it encourages people to trust the process, work hard and keep pushing forward no matter what life throws at them. The song has not yet been released. An official release date is expected to be announced soon.

items.title: Multidimensional Poverty Index to inform next DACF formula – Local Gov’t Ministry
items.description: The Local Government Ministry says data from the Ghana Statistical Service’s Multidimensional Poverty Index will be considered in determining the next District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) allocation formula. Director of Local Governance and Decentralisation at the Ministry, Pln. Samuel Seth Passah, says the move is intended to make the distribution of the Fund more responsive to the specific development challenges facing districts. Speaking at a GDCA-JoyNews national dialogue on the Comprehensive Study on DACF Allocation Equity and Guideline Implementation in Ghana (2020–2025), he said the government was considering ways to move beyond general allocation guidelines to address the different needs of individual assemblies. “We have had a meeting with the Ghana Statistical Service, with the Director of Statistics presenting to us the multidimensional poverty index. And that will be taken into account in the next formula,” he said. He explained that the existing guidelines were not rigid and allowed assemblies to seek waivers based on their specific circumstances. However, he said there was a need to make the guidelines more responsive to the priorities of individual districts rather than applying largely generic spending requirements. “The conversation now is to take cognisance of issues of poverty. Yes, we agree. Take cognisance of issues of what specific district needs, not generic,” he said. Mr Passah disclosed that the ministry was considering developing more specific guidelines for individual assemblies to ensure that DACF allocations address their actual development priorities. He said a recent meeting with the Fund’s administrator had also discussed the possibility of going further to identify the specific needs of each district. “Perhaps we even go granular to have specificity for each district. It’s a guideline. So we give guidelines to each of the districts, their needs and what they require the money for, but we also ensure accountability,” he said. On the constitutional provision for the Fund, Mr Passah explained that Article 252 of the 1992 Constitution requires not less than five per cent of Ghana’s total revenue to be allocated to the DACF for development at the local level. He argued that the provision establishes a minimum threshold and provides room for the country to consider whether the share allocated to local authorities should increase. He said the resources were intended to support essential municipal services such as sanitation, drainage, markets and other infrastructure that directly affect communities. Mr Passah added that the DACF allocation formula was submitted to Parliament for approval, after which the Ministers responsible for Local Government and Finance issue guidelines for its utilisation in accordance with Section 126 of the Local Governance Act. He said the ongoing dialogue presented an opportunity to strengthen the Fund’s responsiveness to local development needs while maintaining accountability in its use.

items.title: COP31: A testament to Africa’s leadership, unity and resolve in the fight for climate justice
items.description: For a farmer battling worsening droughts and the coastal community threatened by rising seas, the outcomes of international climate negotiations carry consequences far beyond conference halls. They are a matter of survival, economic security and the right to a future free from the devastating impacts of climate change. As the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) drew to a close after nearly 48 hours of overtime negotiations, the summit concluded without consensus on a Cover Decision. Yet, amidst global diplomatic stalemate, African nations emerged with unprecedented leadership, continental unity, and an uncompromising commitment to fight for climate justice. A cover decision summarizes political priorities, signals collective intent, and sets high-level goals across or beyond formal agenda items, adopted by consensus. Throughout the summit, Africa delivered a unified message to the global community that climate finance is paramount, and policy implementation is impossible without the necessary means of implementation. From the opening plenaries to the final negotiations in Antalya, the African Group of Negotiators (AGN) stood firm in asserting that climate commitments must translate into accessible, predictable public finance. Leaders stressed that the persistent gap between historical pledges and actual delivery directly threatens millions of lives across the Global South. Delivering a Ministerial Statement on behalf of the AGN, Ghana’s Minister for Environment, Science and Technology, Dr. Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, articulated Africa’s core stance that “climate justice cannot remain a promise deferred. We are not asking for charity, but for fairness, accountability and the fulfilment of commitments already made”. Dr. Zanetor cautioned developed nations against mistaking Africa’s commitment to multilateral diplomacy for complacency. “Africa’s continued presence at the negotiating table must never be mistaken for an endless willingness to accept inaction. Every delay has a human cost, and we must never lose sight of the millions of lives and livelihoods at stake,” she stated. Under the strategic leadership of AGN Chair, Nana Dr. Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, African negotiators resisted pressure to rubber-stamp proposals that weakened financial obligations or omitted concrete adaptation finance floors, including the proposed $120 billion annual adaptation floor by 2035. Addressing concerns over the negotiation process and long-term finance, Dr. Amoah emphasized that international climate negotiations must strictly adhere to multilateral principles. “The process must remain Party-driven, and the positions of Parties must be meaningfully considered,” he insisted. Dr. Amoah noted that long-term finance discussions lacked sufficient space for true negotiation, and called on the Standing Committee on Finance (SCF) to adopt methodological frameworks that build trust and accurately reflect financial provision and mobilization. The summit also witnessed moments of sharp diplomatic tension. When Africa’s collective statement was rudely interrupted during the closing plenary, Dr. Amoah made a principled intervention in defense of Ghana and the AGN, prompting an official apology from COP31 President Murat Kurum. Reflecting on the incident, Dr. Zanetor noted that “diplomacy must be grounded in mutual respect, inclusivity and the equal dignity of every nation… Climate diplomacy must be more than negotiations; it must reflect fairness, respect and genuine partnership”. Civil society organizations across Africa strongly backed the AGN’s firm stance against retrogressive texts that deleted explicit fossil fuel phase-out commitments and stripped funding from just transition mechanisms. Baboucarr Sufism Nyang Al-Tijani, Coordinator of Climate Action Network in the Gambia, commended the resilience of African representatives. He said, “While the failure to agree on the Cover Decision is deeply disappointing, Africa’s leadership, unity and commitment throughout these negotiations deserve to be celebrated. The outcome may have failed our people, but African leadership did not fail in its responsibility to fight for climate justice.” Executive Director of the Pan African Climate Justice Alliance (PACJA), Dr. Mithika Mwenda, also underscored that rejecting an inadequate text was necessary to protect vulnerable communities. “What collapsed on the plenary floor in Antalya today was an attempt by historical emitters and fossil fuel interests to force developing nations to accept an empty shell… While the breakdown of talks is a bitter indictment of global climate diplomacy, rejecting a retrogressive deal prevents a dangerous step backwards,” he stated. Reflecting on the summit’s collapse, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary, Simon Stiell, acknowledged the deep disappointment felt by delegates while calling for renewed resolve. “Our process must follow the science and meet the challenge… This process belongs to 194 Parties. Consensus works best from the ground up… The fight continues. We will never give up,” he said. With COP31 concluded, the center of global climate diplomacy shifts directly to African soil, as Ethiopia prepares to host COP32 in Addis Ababa in November 2027. Chair of the Political and Technical Affairs Committee of PACJA, Dr. Augustine Njamshi, urged African leaders to turn the outcome in Antalya into a rallying point for continental resource mobilization. “Antalya must serve as a wake-up call for African leaders and the global community,” he stated. “As the COP gavel moves to Addis Ababa next year, Africa must not become a dumping ground for COP31’s unfinished business. We must mobilise domestic and regional resources, protect our ecosystems and communities, and build an unshakeable continental front that demands enforceable public finance and genuine climate justice in 2027.”

items.title: Gaza : une boussole morale. Avec Aymeric Caron
items.description: Les crimes commis par les autorités israéliennes envers la population de Gaza, régulièrement qualifiés de génocide par plusieurs ONG, imposent progressivement une frontière morale entre ceux qui les cautionnent et ceux qui les dénoncent. De nombreux États ou personnalités publiques restent silencieux face à ces évènements, alors même que les violences de masse perpétrées envers les populations les plus vulnérables (enfants, femmes et personnes âgées) sont un fait documenté qui constitue une atteinte fondamentale aux droits humains. Cette absence de considération pour les victimes est amplifiée par la silenciation des voix palestiniennes, tant dans les médias privés que publics. Cette crise morale est symptomatique de la dérive d’un monde occidental qui s’écarte des principes qu’il prétend porter : alors même qu’il revendique la défense des droits humains et des libertés individuelles, l’Occident est frappé par l’affaiblissement de la démocratie, la montée de l’extrême droite et plus largement la multiplication des atteintes au vivant. Comment expliquer que le conflit israélo-palestinien ait un tel impact sur les rapports sociaux ? L’impunité israélienne à Gaza est-elle le symptôme d’un effondrement moral de l’Occident ? Comment qualifier l’omerta qui règne autour de la question palestinienne dans les médias ? Quel lien peut-on établir entre le combat pour les droits humains et l’antispécisme ? Autant d'enjeux abordés avec Aymeric Caron, ancien reporter, député de Paris et fondateur du parti Révolution écologique pour le vivant (REV). L’article Gaza : une boussole morale. Avec Aymeric Caron est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: Colas interminables para votar por correo en la recta final de la campaña electoral: “Esto es bárbaro”
items.description: Carlos Pinon es un malagueño de 22 años que se ha tenido que enfrentar a una larga fila para depositar su voto por correo. Con sus muletas, sentado, observa desde una esquina más de un centenar de personas que se encuentran delante de él en la oficina ubicada en la madrileña calle de Guzmán el Bueno, en el distrito de Moncloa-Aravaca. Es la segunda vez que vota. En 2023 respaldó a Pedro Sánchez. Después se mudó a la capital para entrenar para los Juegos Paralímpicos de Los Ángeles 2028, y desde aquí confía en que su voto para Feijóo marcará la diferencia. “Tiene que haber un cambio porque hay cosas que se pueden hacer mejor”, ha destacado. Aunque el candidato popular y el líder de Vox han desconfiado de las garantías del voto por correo , 1.099.687 personas lo han solicitado, un 11,47% más que en las generales de 2019 y un 58,07% menos que en las de 2023, que coincidieron con las vacaciones de verano. items.title: Salon de l’Investissement Sénégal-Belgique : Dakar veut transformer les transferts de sa diaspora en investissements durables
items.description: Les 11 et 12 décembre, la capitale belge accueillera le Salon de l’investissement Sénégal-Belgique (Siseb 2026), un forum pensé pour transformer les transferts financiers des expatriés en projets immobiliers et productifs durables. C’est une manne financière considérable, mais encore trop souvent freinée par les lourdeurs administratives et les craintes de litiges fonciers. Les 11 et 12 décembre prochains, la diaspora sénégalaise de Belgique et d’Europe tentera de lever ces obstacles à l’occasion du Salon de l’investissement Sénégal-Belgique (Siseb 2026), qui se tiendra à Bruxelles, selon un communiqué Initiée par l’Observatoire des Sénégalais de la diaspora (Osd), avec l’appui stratégique de l’ambassade du Sénégal en Belgique et au Luxembourg, cette rencontre économique entend réunir un large éventail d’acteurs. D’après la note des organisateurs, décideurs publics sénégalais, promoteurs immobiliers, établissements financiers, mais aussi investisseurs belges, Africains et membres de la communauté expatriée y prendront part. L’objectif est double, puisqu’il s’agit à la fois de consolider les passerelles économiques entre Dakar et Bruxelles et de canaliser l’épargne des Sénégalais de l’extérieur vers le développement national. Placée sous le thème « Habitat et investissement de la diaspora », cette édition mettra en lumière le rôle stratégique des émigrés dans le financement du logement au Sénégal, précise le document. Pour passer des intentions aux actes, informe l’a note, les échanges s’articuleront autour de l’accès au crédit, des mécanismes de financement de l’habitat et, surtout, de la sécurisation juridique des acquisitions immobilières, un point névralgique pour quiconque investit à distance. Toutefois, les initiateurs de l’événement veulent élargir l’horizon au-delà du seul secteur du bâtiment. Par le truchement de cette initiative, l’Osd souhaite encourager les investissements productifs et les transferts d’expertise dans d’autres filières jugées prioritaires, à commencer par l’agro-industrie et les services financiers, indique le communiqué. Une manière de faire émerger de nouvelles synergies durables entre les deux pays, portées par une diaspora envisagée comme un levier économique à part entière. Pathé NIANG

items.title: Fury vs Joshua: UK council approves 3am finish despite residents’ objections
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Cardiff councillors have approved plans allowing the Tyson Fury versus Anthony Joshua fight at the Principality Stadium to run into the early hours of December 12, despite residents’ concerns over noise, antisocial behaviour and public safety. According to the BBC, Cardiff Council’s Licensing Sub Committee approved a one-night extension allowing hospitality boxes to serve alcohol until 3am, with the stadium closing at 3.30am. The fight is scheduled for December 11, with the ring walk expected at 1am and the opening bell at about 1.30am to accommodate prime-time television coverage in the United States. The committee was told that 130 police officers and 1,600 stewards would be deployed. Some 450 stewards will be assigned to spectators seated on the stadium pitch. None of the residents who objected attended the meeting. South Wales Police Chief Inspector Huw Thomas said the length of the programme meant officers were treating it as a “three-day event”. Stadium director Mark Williams said organisers were expecting a capacity crowd of 77,000 if all tickets sold. Measures to address concerns include additional early-morning trains, noise monitoring and no external public address system. Breathalysers will be used at stadium entrances for spectators who appear intoxicated. Committee chair Grace Ferguson-Thorne said the security arrangements, stewarding levels and planned closure of the stadium roof were “really reassuring”. The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before. Joe Calzaghe’s 2007 victory over Mikkel Kessler began at about 2am to suit US television audiences. Anthony Joshua’s 2018 fight against Joseph Parker drew more than 78,000 spectators, setting an attendance record for the venue. items.title: AJK Assembly sets conditions for resumption of dialogue with proscribed JAAC
items.description: MUZAFFARABAD: The Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Legislative Assembly on Wednesday offered to reopen negotiations with the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), subject to the disbandment of armed groups, surrender of those allegedly involved in serious crimes and an unequivocal commitment to pursue demands through constitutional and democratic means. The region has witnessed violence-marred protests over the past few months, particularly in June and July, with reports of sporadic unrest in recent weeks. At the root of the tensions was JAAC’s demand to abolish the 12 refugee seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly. Adopting a resolution unanimously, the House on Wednesday also demanded an end to all sit-ins and illegal protests, reopening of highways and other routes, and a public apology by JAAC’s leadership for what it described as anti-state narratives directed against state institutions, law enforcement personnel, Pakistan and the Kashmir freedom movement. The resolution, jointly moved by Deputy Speaker Mohammad Ahmed Raza Qadri, Forests Minister Waqar Ahmed Noor, Health Minister Dr Mustafa Bashir Abbasi, Education Minister Umair Naeem, Energy and Water Resources Minister Saqib Majeed Raja and MLA Chaudhry Mohammad Ismail, was read out by Noor. The sitting was presided over by Speaker Chaudhry Tariq Farooq . The House said the AJK government would be prepared to resume meaningful political dialogue with the committee within the framework of the Interim Constitution of 1974 and relevant laws if the stipulated conditions were met. It maintained that a lasting solution to political disputes lay in constitutional means, the rule of law and mutual respect rather than violence and confrontation. The resolution held the JAAC leadership primarily responsible for the breakdown of negotiations , claiming that the government had accepted several of its demands and provided assurances on others despite violent protests. It alleged that JAAC had subsequently interpreted the government’s concessions and flexibility as weakness and raised unconstitutional demands incompatible with the existing constitutional and democratic structure of AJK. The resolution further said the government had also offered several alternative avenues for resolving the dispute, including high-level negotiations, participation in a multi-party conference and the general elections, seeking the AJK Supreme Court’s opinion on constitutional questions through a reference, and holding a referendum on important constitutional matters. The JAAC leadership, however, had rejected these options, the resolution claimed. The assembly expressed grave concern over what it described as attempts to disrupt the timely holding of general elections and create anarchy and uncertainty in the state through armed groups and violent marches since June 2026 . It accused elements affiliated with JAAC of obstructing the movement of law enforcement agencies (LEAs), blocking highways, attacking hospitals, threatening government officials, establishing armed checkpoints and causing the closure of universities, medical colleges, schools and other public institutions. The resolution also alleged that armed groups had obstructed the supply of essential commodities, opened fire with sophisticated weapons and carried out lethal attacks on law enforcement personnel. It particularly condemned the alleged desecration of the bodies of police personnel martyred during the unrest and restrictions imposed on the movement of ordinary citizens through armed checkpoints. The House said the violence had severely disrupted normal life, caused shortages of essential commodities and forced women, children and elderly people to leave affected areas for the safety of their lives and property. Access to education and healthcare, freedom of movement and protection of life and property had also been affected, it added. According to figures placed before the assembly, 34 LEA personnel had been martyred and 248 injured during the unrest, which erupted in June. The assembly paid tribute to all those martyred and expressed condolences and solidarity with their bereaved families. At the same time, the House made a distinction between the right to peaceful protest and unlawful activities, reiterating that peaceful demonstrations, political dissent and constitutional rights were fundamental entitlements of citizens, which the state was bound to protect. It maintained that these rights could not be used as a cover for armed violence, holding citizens hostage, damaging public and private property, blocking highways or attacking state institutions. The resolution echoed the then-AJK government’s allegations that the JAAC leadership had used social media to promote a narrative contrary to facts and exaggerate casualties, spreading anxiety and speculation among Pakistanis and Kashmiris living abroad. The resolution warned that in case of non-compliance with its demands, the AJK government should discharge its constitutional responsibilities by taking necessary legal action through LEAs to restore state authority, maintain public order and protect citizens’ lives and property. Such action, it stressed, must remain within the bounds of the Constitution, law and human rights. The House also paid tribute to the historic contributions of the people of Poonch to the Kashmir freedom movement, expressing the expectation that they would help maintain peace, stability and the rule of law in the region. Reaffirming its commitment to preserving the existing administrative and constitutional structure of AJK, the assembly said the state’s peaceful, stable and democratic character was essential not only for safeguarding the rights and collective interests of its people but also for the broader objectives of the Kashmir freedom movement. It resolved that political differences and public demands would be addressed through dialogue and constitutional means, but there would be no compromise on the rule of law, state authority and the protection of public life and property. Additionally, the House approved three resolutions tabled by treasury members Pir Mazhar Saeed and Sehrish Qamar, as well as Opposition Leader Chaudhry Muhammad Yasin. Through their respective motions, Saeed called for displaying Quranic verses affirming the finality of prophethood in the Assembly hall, Qamar welcomed the recent visit of the PML-N leadership to Muzaffarabad, and Yasin paid tribute to former president Raja Zulqarnain Khan. On June 5, following the announcement of the JAAC’s June 9 strike, the then-PPP-led AJK government declared the committee a proscribed organisation and placed it under the First Schedule of the region’s anti-terrorism act (ATA). A day later, AJK authorities launched a crackdown on the JAAC, arresting scores of its leaders and later placing scores of its activists on the Fourth Schedule of the ATA. Elections in the region were held in three phases on July 27 , Aug 2 and Aug 10 amid protests in some parts. The PML-N — which leads the coalition in the Centre — emerged as the winner. Earlier this month, AJK President Dr Muhammad Najeeb and Prime Minister Iftikhar Gillani called for restraint and peace, with the latter observing that provocative discourse and prevailing unrest were disrupting the lives of ordinary people. The remarks came days after the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) expressed its concern over “reports of a fresh spate of violence in Rawalakot in AJK, with allegations of casualties among both protesters and law enforcement personnel”. It called for the media to be “given unhindered access to report from the region independently”. “The priority must be to prevent any loss of life and resolve the situation through political dialogue rather than by force,” HRCP stressed.

items.title: Obi to meet Aba traders, artisans, manufacturers Friday – Nwaogu
items.description: By Ugochukwu Alaribe UMUAHIA — The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, will hold a town hall meeting with traders, manufacturers, artisans and youths in Aba, Abia State, on Friday, November 27. The Abia State Coordinator of the NDC, Senator Nkechi Nwaogu, disclosed this while briefing journalists in Aba, saying the visit would provide an opportunity for business owners and other residents to engage directly with the presidential candidate. Nwaogu, who is also the party’s senatorial candidate for Abia Central, said Obi’s visit, alongside his running mate, Senator Musa Kwankwaso, would attract a large crowd. She predicted that the turnout would surpass the crowd recorded during Obi’s visit to Onitsha the previous week. According to her, although the primary purpose of the visit is to hold a town hall meeting, Obi will also move around Aba to interact with residents. She added that the NDC presidential candidate would return to the city between December and January for an open-air campaign. Nwaogu said the meeting would provide traders, manufacturers, shoemakers, tailors and young people with an opportunity to discuss the challenges facing businesses and the economy with Obi. “Our brothers and sisters in Aba, the business heartbeat of Nigeria, will have the opportunity to sit, eat and discuss with Peter Obi. He will listen to the traders, manufacturers, shoemakers, tailors and youths. He wants to hear how we can rebuild Aba, revive trade and make businesses work again,” she said. The NDC coordinator expressed concern over unemployment, the difficulties confronting businesses, the declining purchasing power of the naira and the state of infrastructure and public services. She said Obi was coming to Abia with proposals focused on production, education, healthcare, security and job creation. “Peter Obi is not coming to Abia just because he is a presidential candidate. He is coming with a plan: a plan for production, not consumption; a plan for education, health, security and jobs; and a plan to ensure that government money is used for the people, rather than taken by a few,” she added. Nwaogu urged security agencies and the Abia State Government to provide the necessary support to ensure a peaceful and successful visit. She said the NDC was committed to peaceful and lawful political activities and would take necessary steps to maintain order throughout the visit. items.title: Meet 3 African countries with churches carved directly into rocks
items.description: Across Africa, early Christian communities left behind extraordinary architecture — not by stacking stones upward, but by carving sacred spaces straight into mountainsides, cliffs, and subterranean bedrock. From subterranean monoliths to massive mountain caves, these three African countries are home to some of the world’s most remarkable rock-hewn churches. Ethiopia Ethiopia is home to the world’s most famous collection of rock-cut churches. In the northern town of Lalibela, 11 medieval monolithic churches were chiseled downward out of solid volcanic rock during the 12th and 13th centuries. The most iconic of them, Biete Giyorgis (Church of Saint George), is carved in the shape of a giant cross and sits inside a deep pit surrounded by trenches and tunnels. Beyond Lalibela, Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region holds more than 120 rock-hewn churches tucked high into sandstone cliffs and mountain peaks, many featuring centuries-old frescoes and requiring steep climbs to reach. Egypt Egypt’s deep Coptic Christian heritage includes striking cave churches and rock-cut sanctuaries carved into desert cliffs and hills. Just outside Cairo, in the Mokattam hills, sits the Monastery of Saint Simon the Tanner — widely known as the Cave Church. Carved directly into the rocky mountainside, its main amphitheater-style sanctuary can hold thousands of worshippers and features intricate biblical scenes sculpted into the stone walls. Further south along the Nile, historic Coptic sites such as the Monastery of the Virgin Mary (Deir el-Adra) in Rifa near Asyut preserve ancient chapels excavated directly out of limestone cliffs. Eritrea Sharing the rugged highlands and early Christian roots of the Horn of Africa, Eritrea also preserves a rich tradition of rock-hewn church architecture. Across the country’s central and southern highlands — particularly in regions like Debub and the areas surrounding Senafe and Adi Keyh — historic churches and monastic chapels were carved directly into rocky outcrops and cliff faces. Sites such as Enda Abune Libanos near Ham and other highland rock sanctuaries reflect centuries of devotion, blending natural stone caverns with hand-carved pillars, arches, and sanctuaries built to endure in remote mountain landscapes.
