Kenya: Gender-based violence: a public health and human rights concern
items.description: Country: Kenya Source: World Health Organization Nairobi— Married at the age of 14, Mparakoni Leabune from Samburu County in northern Kenya was the third wife in a polygamous union. “My husband used to beat me a lot," she says. "That is how I got this leg injury," she says pointing to severe swelling on her left leg. Despite countless medical interventions, Leabune has endured a long and painful road to recovery. "My husband divorced me and now I live with my mother," she says. Aside from enduring physical violence, Leabune is a survivor of early marriage, which is also considered a form of gender-based violence. According to Kenya’s 2022 Demographic Health Survey, more than a third of women (34%) in Kenya have experienced physical violence since the age of 15 years, and 13% have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime. Nine out of 10 times, the perpetrator is a either a current or former husband or partner. Furthermore, according to the 2025/2026 Kenya Mini-Demographic Heath Survey, technology- facilitated gender-based violence is on the rise: more than a quarter of women aged age 15–49 have ever experienced it from any perpetrator. Technology- facilitated gender-based violence includes acts such as online harassment, cyberbullying and online control to cause harm. “Women are suffering silently because they cannot seek medical attention, not because of their own will, but because of the patriarchal society we live in," says Samson Esward Leerte, nurse and reproductive health coordinator for adolescents and young people in Samburu County. The 2010 Constitution protects people in Kenya from harmful cultural practices and violence. Several laws have been enacted and most recently, the National Policy on Gender-based Violence and the National Policy for the Eradication of Female Genital Mutilation were adopted in 2019. The country is taking steps to ramp up implementation of these laws. In January 2025, President Williams Ruto established a technical working group on gender-based violence, including femicide. In November 2025, he heard its recommendations. They include several recommendations to curb femicide and female genital mutilation and operationalizing one-stop gender-based violence recovery centres in every county. In July 2026, the Government of Kenya, through the State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action under the Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services and partners convened a national consultative forum on the implementation of the recommendations and sustainability. "The Ministry of Health remains committed to strengthening the health sector's role in preventing and responding to gender-based violence. Our priority is to ensure that women and girls can access timely, quality and survivor-centred services, while strengthening prevention, early identification, referral and coordination across the health system and with other sectors," says Mary Gathitu, Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Programme Lead at Kenya's Ministry of Health. "Ultimately, protecting women and girls from violence requires sustained, coordinated action at both national and county levels." World Health Organization (WHO) has supported Ministry of Health to conduct assessments of health facility readiness to respond to gender-based violence cases in six counties and has trained more than 250 health workers on the clinical management of gender-based violence survivors since 2025. The Organization also sits on the technical working group that provides support to Ministry of Health on gender-based violence interventions. “Gender-based violence, particularly intimate partner and sexual violence, is a major public health and human rights concern, rooted in unequal gender norms and power dynamics," says Dr. Rita Arogo, Maternal and Reproductive Health Officer at WHO Kenya. "Its prevention and elimination must be elevated as a priority for action and advocacy at the highest levels." Media contacts Genna Print Communication officer WHO Kenya Tel: +254 740 466 426 Email: printg@who.int Saida Swaleh Communications and Media Relations Officer WHO Regional Office for Africa Email: saida.swaleh@who.int

items.title: What Could Replace the Trump Style of Politics?
items.description: J onathan Spector’s play Birthright , which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel. In the last act, which takes place in 2024, the nearly two-decade bond between a group of American Jewish friends has frayed over Gaza. Izzy, the most left-wing of the bunch, has already abandoned their online group chat, where the friends shared photos of their newborn children, checked in during COVID, and planned their reunions. Thrown together for a funeral, Izzy and another friend, Chaya, begin to argue—as one does these days—about Zionism. They quickly whip out their phones, mustering evidence. “Theodor Herzl colonialism,” Izzy types into the search window, which—in an ingenious bit of stagecraft—appears projected on the wall behind her and starts to flow with online sources. “1930s partition plan Israel,” Chaya counter-Googles. They start scrolling through newspaper articles and Wikipedia pages, hurling raw historical information at each other like malfunctioning robots. But no one is listening. Their friend Noah, watching from the side, offers that going to the internet to prove your point is useless because you’ll invariably find what you’re looking for—“which is why I think this is really, really not a good way to go about having an actual conversation.” This mode of political discourse is surely familiar: the search for a truth that will detonate like an atom bomb, ripping the roof off every other truth. Most of us know that this outcome never, ever happens. But beneath the awareness of information bubbles and fake news, of epistemic breakdown, lies a stubbornly common belief that total victory is achievable. This fantasy has even become its own kind of entertainment—think of Jubilee Media ’s viral videos in which one person has to fend off 20 political opponents like a medieval knight, or the late Charlie Kirk ’s “Prove Me Wrong” college tours. Theories are packed tight with facts and lobbed back and forth in what the German philosopher Hannah Arendt once called “an orgy of truth-telling.” Arendt used this strange phrase in a 1946 letter to the philosopher Gershom Scholem, her dear intellectual sparring partner, after they had gotten into a fierce argument about—what else?—Zionism. One shouldn’t be a “fanatic for truth,” Arendt told him. All this did was harden people in their positions: I have my truth, you have yours, and the only way forward is for you to admit that not just your opinions but your facts are wrong . This is no way to hold a debate, or to conduct politics; all it does is create stasis or even worse. Elsewhere, Arendt called truth in this context “despotic.” She argued instead for a different mode, one that would be surprising—okay, maybe fantastical—to consider today: “an orgy of friendship.” In a recently published book, A World We Share , Roger Berkowitz explores the German philosopher’s thoughts on friendship “as the lens through which she understood politics.” For Arendt, who is best known for her hard-bitten analysis of totalitarianism, friendship might seem to be an uncharacteristically schmaltzy subject, but as filtered through her mind, abstracted and held apart, it sheds all Hallmark associations. Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center for Politics and Humanities at Bard College, provides the material for an intriguing thought experiment, one that might be useful as Americans rub their eyes in the post-midterms dawn. After a decade in which Donald Trump’s tribalist instincts have only accelerated that rush to Google-dueling, it might be worth pursuing Arendt’s idea that friendship, as opposed to truth-telling, is a better model for conducting politics. A rendt never left behind a treatise on friendship, but references to the concept pop up throughout her work and letters. Berkowitz, who has a granular familiarity with her writing, brings all of the strands together. For Arendt, friendship is distinct from love as we often think of it; it is not about losing yourself in order to meld with another person and separate from the rest of the world. Instead, this kind of connection preserves difference and feeds off plurality. Friendship is actually the most worldly of relationships because it forces us to accommodate the separateness of the people we know and care about. [ Read: It’s the morality, stupid ] Arendt articulated three defining features: time spent knowing each other (“a two-week-old friendship does not exist,” she said); talking and more talking and even more talking; and a respect and appreciation for the unique conditions that shape someone else’s worldview. This kind of friendship, she thought, should withstand even the most violent disagreements. “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions,” she wrote in her letter to Scholem, begging that they not lose their connection despite her public disillusionment with the idea of an exclusively Jewish state—a critique Scholem must have felt as a body blow. Berkowitz points out that for Arendt, what makes us human “is not our ability to reason or our grasp of moral certainty or absolute truth but our ability to form lasting and meaningful relationships grounded in mutual recognition and respect.” The fact that she and Scholem had spent more than a decade talking, listening, and yelling was more important to her than any need for them to come to similar conclusions. Her emphasis was rather on this “in-between,” the “common world” they shared and built just by continuing to engage on the issues that mattered to them both. Could any of this possibly be applicable to America’s political culture, which most days resembles the fear and loathing of trench warfare? Dream with me for a minute. Imagine if arguments at Thanksgiving dinner or in Congress proceeded with an awareness that conquering the other person’s worldview was impossible—in the way you can’t really change that old friend who keeps dating the wrong people. Imagine if the goal was to tease out commonalities, instead of trying to will the differences away. This type of politics would be fueled by persuasion, as opposed to force or truth, Berkowitz writes; it would aim “neither at domination nor certainty. It is not about being right.” Arendt’s favored metaphor for this in-between is a table around which people with disparate views and interests sit. The existence of the table matters more than anyone’s particular opinions. The American version of this table does exist, however alienated we may feel from one another. The changing state of the economy, for example, or the future of children’s education, are issues that could potentially be served at this table. Some topics—say, abortion rights—would produce more heat, maybe some fist-pounding. But if the objective is to make sure that the table itself doesn’t evaporate, the conversation might continue. Certain shared worries from our shared world will present themselves as commonalities, even as people’s perspectives remain distinct. Take the proliferation of data centers or the cost of health care. “By talking about what is between them,” Arendt writes, friends and citizens can make that shared world “ever more common.” [ Read: Why we should read Hannah Arendt now ] This is what an orgy of friendship (as opposed to one of truth) could look like. I don’t have any illusions that this shift of mindset is easy. But some politicians could point the way—for instance Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas. “I really do believe that the key to saving the American experiment is loving our enemies,” he recently told Michelle Goldberg at The New York Times . “How do we love each other through our disagreements? How do we remember each other’s humanity? How do we handle each other with more care?” Talarico gives this a Christian gloss with his talk of “love,” which is not quite what Arendt had in mind, but she would otherwise be sympathetic to his willingness to make friends with those who have been calling him “Talafreako” for the past year. Of course, going to Washington could very well crush this friendliness out of him, but it is worth paying attention to how rhetorically effective his approach has been. F or anyone who might be rolling their eyes at the idea of friendship and politics occupying even the same sentence, I have two important caveats, both integral to Arendt’s thinking. First, Arendt was not some kind of postmodern relativist; she believed that truth exists and was deeply invested in it. Facts are what make a shared world possible in the first place; they are the floor on which that table stands. If her friendship metaphor seems implausible today, that might be because this basic prerequisite—that political actors agree on the contours of reality—often feels absent. Arendt’s answer to this problem would be to search outside politics for what she called the “truthtellers”—journalists and lawyers, scientists and artists, historians and philosophers. (I can only imagine the despair she’d feel at the idea that these backstops of democratic society are now often dismissed as out-of-touch elites.) The second caveat is that friendship has its limits. Arendt was not suggesting that every disagreement can be overcome, or that preserving a relationship is always the highest good. Some people, and some ideas, are so destructive that they threaten the very possibility of living together. There is a difference between disagreeing about what the world should look like and refusing to recognize that other people have a place in it. Arendt understood this distinction well. She had barely gotten out of Nazi Germany alive. After the war, she had to delineate these limits of friendship on a personal level: Should she reconnect with Germans who had allied with the Nazis? According to Berkowitz, she made an interesting rule for herself. Those who had acquiesced to the Nazis only in the early years, until the Nuremberg Laws were passed in 1935, but then recoiled from where Hitler was headed, she could reconcile with. They “were not all murderers,” she said. With these friends, she told a television interviewer in 1963, “it seemed to me that there should be a basis for communication precisely in the abyss of Auschwitz.” But when it came to those who continued supporting the party after Kristallnacht in 1938, when its genocidal intent became evident, there was no table to speak of. The line is not always so obvious. Arendt’s own ambivalence over Martin Heidegger , her onetime mentor and lover, is revealing. Heidegger, the great philosopher, joined the Nazi Party and lent it his intellectual support; as the rector of his university, he even stripped his own mentor, Edmund Husserl, of his position there because he was Jewish. When exactly Heidegger stopped believing in the cause and started seeing it as “the greatest stupidity of my life,” as he later put it, is not clear. Arendt wouldn’t speak to him again until 1950, and she never publicly forgave him. But she did find a way to reconcile with him, and even renew their friendship. As Berkowitz put it, she decided that the world was better with Heidegger in it. This might seem at first like softness toward an old flame, but it wasn’t; her magnanimity looked like the result of disciplined reasoning. I’m not sure I could have ever spoken to him again, but I can respect that giving the benefit of the doubt seemed to be part of her ethic. This bears keeping in mind at a moment when a friend can be lost over whether he or she is willing to utter the word genocide . [ Read: What is Zionism? ] Arendt herself knew what it meant to be ostracized for one’s political positions. After the publication in 1963 of Eichmann in Jerusalem , her account of the trial of Adolf Eichmann, a key orchestrator of the Holocaust, she was roundly attacked—in part for describing Eichmann’s brand of evil as “banality,” but even more for the perception that she blamed the Jews for their own suffering and was insufficiently horrified by what befell them. In her responses to the many incensed letters and calls for her excommunication, she repeatedly insists on friendship. This willingness to hold differences of opinion while maintaining a relationship even shows up in a novel about Arendt that was rereleased this month. In 1983, Arthur A. Cohen published An Admirable Woman , whose protagonist is an Arendt doppelgänger named Erika Hertz. She too is a German Jewish intellectual who escapes Nazism and becomes a celebrated thinker in New York. To add to the book’s hall-of-mirrors effect, at the very end we discover that Erika Hertz is actually friends with none other than Hannah Arendt. Hertz also takes issue with Eichmann in Jerusalem , but unlike so many others, she refuses to abandon Arendt over it. “I think this is reckless,” Hertz says to herself about the book. And yet she also declares: “I will surely come to her aid.” The two judgments sit side by side. Neither cancels the other out. The point of friendship is not to confirm our view of the world. Hertz sees in Arendt a near copy of herself, and so she isn’t repulsed by this reminder of their separateness. Instead, it reinforces how much they need each other: “Rather than resemble, it is that we dissemble each other. My friend and I. I lie in the folds of her garments. She in mine.” In real life, Arendt was deeply hurt by the friends who threatened to denounce and disavow her. Scholem, her old pen pal, was one of those who found himself on the cusp of saying goodbye to her forever. He judged that her account of the trial had betrayed a lack of ahavath Israel , “love of the Jewish people.” Arendt didn’t flinch. The warmth and connection that people could generate between themselves mattered to her above any other allegiance: “How right you are that I have no such love, and for two reasons: first, I have never in my life ‘loved’ any people or collective, neither the German nor the French nor the American, also not the working class or any other. I love in fact only my friends.”

items.title: Somalia: FLER activation: IDP assessment and community consultations in Afgooye District, Lower Shabelle Region (21 September 2026)
items.description: Country: Somalia Sources: Norwegian Refugee Council, SOS Children's Villages International Please refer to the attached file. Executive Summary Between 29 August and 13 September 2026, intensified security operations and armed confrontations in parts of Lower Shabelle, including Basra, Alifow, Baqdaad and Areer Mooge, displaced more than 860 households (approximately 5,100 people, including about 3,640 children) towards Afgooye and surrounding communities, according to cluster/ABC reporting. An estimated 620 children are currently out of school. SOS Children’s Villages Somalia conducted a field visit and community dialogue in four IDP locations in Lafoole (Waafi, Docol, Durdur and Takulo) to verify the presence of newly displaced families, understand education and protection needs, and identify potential FLER sites. The assessment identified 402 newly displaced households. Education is the most urgent gap: existing public schools are located approximately 1 km to more than 3 km from the settlements, and children who remain out of school face heightened risks of abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour, family separation, early marriage and psychosocial distress. Immediate FLER activation is therefore strongly justified. FLER will provide safe, structured learning, psychosocial support, play and life-skills activities, foundational learning and protection identification and referral, while creating a pathway into neighbouring schools. Docol and Durdur IDP Community Centres are the priority FLER locations, covering multiple surrounding IDP subcamps.

items.title: California grand jury indicts Meghan Markle's estranged father on child porn charges
items.description: The estranged father of Meghan Markle, wife of Britain’s Prince Harry, was indicted by a California grand jury on Tuesday on two counts of possession of child pornography. Thomas Markle, 82, who is already in custody in Florida after removing the ankle monitor that had been attached as a condition of house arrest, is expected to be arraigned in the United States District Court in Los Angeles in the coming weeks. The indictment alleges that Markle had 35mm negatives showing child sexual abuse, including at least one image involving a prepubescent minor. Court documents allege Markle had illegal photographs both in the Philippines, where he had previously lived, and in two rented storage facilities in Los Angeles. Prosecutors said FBI agents seized dozens of images on slides, film negatives and in books, including two that appear to depict Markle with children who are either naked or in various states of undress. A Florida judge this month ordered that Markle undergo a psychiatric examination after finding “reasonable cause to believe” that he was suffering from a condition “rendering him mentally incompetent to the extent that he is unable to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him or to assist properly in his defence”. Philippines seeks charges Philippine authorities filed criminal complaints against Markle last week in Cebu, where he is said to have lived for over a year, regional prosecutor Graeme Elmido said. Police recommended that Markle be charged with two counts of distributing child sexual abuse material and one count of possessing such material under Philippine law. “The complaints will go through preliminary evaluation,” Elmido said. “If the evidence warrants… a regular preliminary investigation subpoena will then be sent to Markle Sr to answer the charges.” Markle’s legal troubles began in October when the British tabloid The Sun reported that his son, Thomas Markle Jr, had discovered child sex abuse images while going through boxes found in his father’s former home in the Philippines. Markle had been living in Cebu until reportedly returning to the United States earlier this year. Meghan Markle said last month that she was “ deeply distressed ” by accusations that her father possessed images of child sexual abuse. She said she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous “troubling and disturbing” allegations. Harry, the second son of King Charles III and estranged brother of the heir to the throne, Prince William, married Meghan, an American former actor, at Windsor Castle in May 2018. The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 but made an unexpected return with their two children to live in the United Kingdom in August.

items.title: World: Preparedness for the next crisis means planning for the one after it
items.description: Country: World Source: ODI - Humanitarian Practice Network Giuseppe Saba As the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon in March 2026 intensified humanitarian needs and displacement, the ability to respond quickly depended in part on decisions made before the emergency. By 1 May 2026, UNHCR reported that, together with shelter sector partners, it had delivered relief items to more than 200,000 displaced people, largely using pre-positioned supplies. Additional support included 40 trucks carrying more than 317 metric tonnes of critical aid from Dubai . Preparedness enabled the response. Stocks, logistics infrastructure and multiple transport options were available before the operating environment deteriorated. This flexibility is increasingly essential in humanitarian logistics. Conflict can escalate while teams are responding to floods elsewhere; a disease outbreak can increase demand as border restrictions constrain supply; and disruption to a single transport route can affect operations far beyond the crisis that caused it. Overlapping emergencies place simultaneous pressure on the same people, supplies, funding and logistics networks. Preparedness must therefore preserve the capacity to adapt under pressure. That requires strategically positioned supplies, alternative routes and suppliers, visibility of available stocks, established cross-sector relationships, and mechanisms that link early warning to early action. These options need to be in place before a response is under strain. Prepare for crises that overlap Other operational lessons from the past six years began with Covid-19. The pandemic showed how quickly disruption in one part of the humanitarian system could propagate across others. Border closures, shifting regulations and competition for transport and essential goods constrained supply chains as demand increased, while humanitarian organisations continued to respond to conflict, displacement, food insecurity and natural hazards. Subsequent crises have reinforced the same lesson. Emergencies overlap, compete for shared resources, and can disrupt the systems needed to respond to one another. Preparedness therefore needs to account for interacting risks and cumulative demand across the humanitarian system. Stress-testing should reflect these conditions: a major transport route becoming unavailable during a disease outbreak; stocks allocated to one response being required for another; or several organisations competing for the same aircraft, warehouse or supplier. These scenarios reveal likely capacity constraints and identify where alternatives need to be established in advance. The practical shift is towards preparing the humanitarian system to operate under cumulative pressure. Organisations need visibility over critical dependencies, the speed at which resources can be redirected, and the decisions required when several responses draw on the same capacity. Pre-position for flexibility Pre-positioning reduces response time and preserves operational flexibility as conditions change. Supplies held in strategically connected locations can be deployed rapidly after a sudden-onset emergency and redirected when borders close, transport capacity contracts, or the original response plan becomes unviable. The February 2023 earthquakes in Türkiye and Syria demonstrated the value of rapid deployment from pre-positioned capacity. Within hours, the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Logistics Centre began mobilising emergency health supplies, and 110 metric tonnes of trauma and surgical supplies were dispatched in the initial response . WHO also drew immediately on supplies already positioned in Syria, showing how stocks at different levels of the supply chain can reinforce one another when response time is critical. The Lebanon response described at the outset demonstrates a second value: preserving operational options as needs and access conditions evolve. In March 2026, 21.5 metric tonnes of WHO medical supplies were also transported overland from pre-positioned UNCHR stocks in Dubai to Lebanon in four trucks to support healthcare assistance for displaced communities . These movements demonstrate the value of regional connectivity, established partnerships and operational readiness. Pre-positioning creates optionality. It gives humanitarian organisations a prepared base from which stocks can be released quickly, transport modes adapted, and assistance kept moving as conditions change. Effective preparedness creates the capacity to respond when an emergency unfolds differently from the original plan. Stock-positioning decisions should therefore weigh historical demand and proximity against connectivity, customs arrangements and alternative onward routes. A well-positioned stockpile enables rapid deployment and preserves viable pathways when the preferred route fails. Design redundancy across the supply chain Supply chains concentrated around a single supplier, port, border crossing or transport route can become critical points of failure during a disruption. Humanitarian organisations need to identify these concentrations and establish credible alternatives for the dependencies that pose the greatest operational risk. Resource constraints make comprehensive duplication unrealistic. Resilience can instead be built by qualifying alternative suppliers in advance, maintaining access to multiple ports or airports, distributing critical stock across locations, and identifying the failures with the greatest operational consequences so that viable alternatives are ready. Redundancy also has a system-wide dimension. The humanitarian system collectively holds substantial stocks, logistics infrastructure and operational capacity across organisations and hubs. Greater visibility and coordination of that capacity can strengthen resilience without requiring each organisation to replicate the same capabilities. Preparedness therefore depends on understanding the capacity available across the wider system, the conditions under which it can be accessed, and the speed at which it can be mobilised. This is particularly important during concurrent emergencies, when an organisation’s own stocks or logistics capacity may already be committed elsewhere. Treat information as preparedness infrastructure Collective capacity is useful only when decision-makers can see what is available. Humanitarian stocks are held across multiple organisations and locations; governments hold customs and movement information; and logistics providers hold data on transport capacity and constraints. Preparedness needs to turn these separate information sources into a usable operational picture before a crisis creates urgent demand for it. The Humanitarian Logistics Databank offers one model . The platform brings together information on humanitarian stocks held across the Dubai Humanitarian hub . By combining data on the quantity, location, ownership and movement of relief supplies, including customs data from ports and airports, the platform gives participating organisations a clearer view of available capacity. This visibility supports faster operational decisions: identifying supplies already positioned near an emerging crisis; determining what needs to be mobilised, rerouted or procured; and understanding what resources may already be available elsewhere in the humanitarian system. Connecting visibility across hubs makes distributed capacity more actionable: agencies can identify existing resources across locations before establishing new supply chains or moving supplies over longer distances. The value increases when several emergencies draw simultaneously on limited stocks and logistics capacity. Scaling this model requires more than technical connectivity. Each new hub must align customs regimes, data-sharing rules and operational mandates across governments, agencies and private operators. Extending shared visibility is therefore a policy and governance challenge as well as a technical one, and progress will depend on sustained institutional alignment. Shared visibility also depends on trust. Participating actors need confidence in data quality, clarity on access and use, and agreed protocols for information sharing. Establishing these arrangements during preparedness enables data to support decisions immediately when a crisis begins. Build relationships before they are tested Preparedness is also relational. Governments, United Nations agencies, international and local organisations, customs authorities, donors and private-sector partners each control capabilities or make decisions that can become critical during an emergency. The Global Health Cluster’s examination of the Covid-19 response highlighted the contributions of civil society, local partners and community leaders, as well as collaboration with government ministries, law enforcement and the private sector. It recommended embedding multisectoral and community-based mechanisms within preparedness so they are operational before a crisis . The same principle applies across emergency types. Established relationships with government and customs authorities can help organisations respond to changing access conditions; relationships with logistics providers can unlock alternative transport capacity; and national and local organisations can sustain access when international teams cannot reach affected communities. These relationships require sustained investment in preparedness planning, joint exercises and regular coordination. Local organisations should be involved early, drawing on their knowledge of communities, access constraints and local risks to shape contingency planning, stock positioning and trigger decisions. This embeds localisation within the preparedness architecture from the outset. Connect early warning to operational readiness Anticipatory action depends on operational preparedness. Credible forecasts and early warnings can trigger evacuation, cash assistance, protective supplies or measures to protect homes and livelihoods, but the system must already be able to convert warning into action. That requires linking forecasts to pre-agreed decisions. If severe flooding is predicted, teams should know who can authorise the release of supplies, whether financing is available before a formal emergency declaration, where relevant stocks are held, which partners can reach at-risk communities, and which threshold triggers the response. Pre-agreed triggers, responsibilities and financing shorten the gap between warning and action. Without them, better forecasting produces earlier awareness, while operational response remains delayed. Forecasting creates a window for earlier action; preparedness determines whether the system has the resources, authority, partnerships and processes to act. Putting the lessons into practice Six years of overlapping crises point to a clear priority: preparedness must be designed for disruption, interaction and change. That means stress-testing for concurrent emergencies, building flexibility into supply chains and pre-positioning, creating visibility of shared capacity, strengthening partnerships in advance, and linking early warning to clear decisions and financing. Successive and overlapping humanitarian crises have reinforced a clear priority: how much of the response architecture was already in place before the crisis escalated? Stocks, data, routes, partnerships and decision-making mechanisms determine how quickly aid can move and whether it can continue to do so as conditions change. Humanitarian resilience will depend on the system’s capacity to adapt when events unfold differently from expectations. Embedding that adaptability in planning, coordination and response should be central to preparedness for the crises ahead.

items.title: Marché des capitaux: près de 87,6 MMDH de levées à fin septembre 2026
items.description: Les levées de capitaux ont atteint près de 87,6 milliards de dirhams (MMDH) à fin septembre 2026, contre 83,73 MMDH à la même période un an auparavant, selon l'Autorité marocaine du marché des capitaux (AMMC). Ces levées comprennent les émissions de titres de créances négociables (TCN) avec près de 65 MMDH, les émissions obligataires (19,45 MMDH) et les émissions de titres en capital (3,14 MMDH), précise l'AMMC dans ses indicateurs mensuels du marché des capitaux de septembre. Concernant l'encours des opérations de prêt emprunt de titres, il s'est établi à 34,5 MMDH à fin septembre dernier, enregistrant une baisse de 35% depuis le début de l'année et de 9% sur les 12 derniers mois. Pour le seul mois de septembre 2026, les levées de capitaux se sont chiffrées à plus de 10,6 MMDH, dont 10,06 MMDH provenant des émissions de TCN, 400 millions de dirhams (MDH) des émissions obligataires et 142 MDH des émissions de titres de capital. The post Marché des capitaux: près de 87,6 MMDH de levées à fin septembre 2026 appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Labé : deux mois sans gaz, les ménages à bout et les prix en roue libre
items.description: Depuis près de deux mois, recharger une bonbonne de gaz domestique relève du véritable parcours du combattant dans la commune urbaine de Labé. Entre ruptures de stock à répétition, spéculation sur les prix et risque d’un retour au bois de chauffe et au charbon, l’inquiétude gagne les ménages. Selon des sources concordantes jointes par Guinéenews, cette situation serait liée à des difficultés d’approvisionnement imputables notamment à des dysfonctionnements au niveau de l’État. « Ces derniers jours, j’ai marché avec ma bonbonne pendant trois jours sans trouver un seul point de recharge. Le seul que j’ai finalement trouvé m’a proposé un prix exorbitant. Pour une bonbonne habituellement rechargée à 60 000 GNF, il m’a réclamé 80 000 GNF. Je n’ai finalement pas accepté. Malheureusement, dès le lendemain, il n’y avait plus de gaz », témoigne Mamadou Lamine Bah. La difficulté est loin d’être un cas isolé. Interrogé par Guinéenews, l’inspecteur régional de l’Environnement, Mamadou Kobera Diallo, affirme être lui aussi confronté à cette situation depuis deux mois, malgré de nombreuses démarches. « Cela fait deux mois que je cherche à recharger ma bonbonne de 12 kilogrammes, mais c’est impossible. J’ai tout essayé, sans succès. Partout où je passe, on me parle de rupture de stock », déplore-t-il. Face à cette situation qui perdure, Mamadou Lamine Bah interpelle les autorités et les invite à prendre des mesures urgentes pour garantir la disponibilité du gaz domestique. « Je ne sais pas exactement ce qui manque, mais l’État doit s’impliquer pour éviter ce genre de rupture. C’est d’autant plus important que la population est en train de délaisser progressivement le charbon et le bois au profit du gaz. Il ne faudrait pas décourager cette transition qui commence à avoir des effets positifs. Des stations de recharge ont été installées dans les grandes villes, notamment à Labé, qui en compte deux. Mais si l’approvisionnement devient impossible, même avec ces deux stations, cela va sérieusement compromettre cette dynamique », prévient-il. Sur le terrain, le sujet semble particulièrement sensible. Aucun responsable de station de recharge de gaz à Labé n’a accepté de répondre aux questions de Guinéenews, par crainte, selon nos informations, de s’exposer à des représailles de sa hiérarchie. En revanche, des sources bien informées évoquent des dysfonctionnements liés au mécanisme de subvention publique. Selon ces interlocuteurs, l’État aurait accumulé plusieurs milliards de francs guinéens d’arriérés auprès des fournisseurs de gaz, poussant ces derniers à suspendre leurs livraisons. Une autre source, qui a requis l’anonymat, confirme que les stations de recharge de la commune urbaine de Labé n’ont pas été ravitaillées depuis deux mois. Pour tenter de satisfaire, tant bien que mal, une partie de la demande locale, certaines citernes seraient contraintes de s'approvisionner au Sénégal voisin. « En plus de la rupture, qui est une réalité, la demande est désormais largement supérieure à l’offre. La population a massivement migré vers le gaz, ce qui a considérablement augmenté les besoins. C’est essentiellement là que se situe le problème. Sinon, le gaz arrive de temps en temps », explique notre interlocuteur. Au-delà des désagréments quotidiens imposés aux ménages, cette pénurie soulève un véritable enjeu environnemental. Sans une réaction rapide des autorités pour sécuriser l’approvisionnement et consolider cette transition vers des combustibles moins polluants, les efforts engagés risquent d'être compromis. Privés durablement de gaz, de nombreux foyers pourraient être contraints de renouer avec le bois de chauffe et le charbon. Une régression qui accentuerait la pression sur les ressources forestières et fragiliserait davantage les efforts de préservation de l'environnement en Guinée.

items.title: CRIEF : faute d’avocats de l’État, le procès d’Ahmed Sékou Traoré renvoyé au 9 décembre
items.description: Le procès pour un présumé détournement de deniers publics à la mairie de Ratoma devra encore attendre. La chambre de jugement de la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (CRIEF) a renvoyé au 9 décembre 2026 l’affaire impliquant Ahmed Sékou Traoré, ancien président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de Ratoma, et Mohamed Camara, ancien receveur communal. Les deux prévenus sont poursuivis pour un présumé détournement de 32 milliards de francs guinéens. Ce renvoi fait suite à une demande de la défense, qui a invoqué l’absence des avocats de l’État guinéen. Ces derniers ont, en effet, suspendu leur participation à l’ensemble des procédures dans lesquelles l’État est constitué partie civile. À l’audience du 2 novembre dernier, Ahmed Sékou Traoré avait catégoriquement rejeté les accusations portées contre lui, notamment le détournement de deniers publics, la corruption, le faux et usage de faux, l’enrichissement illicite et le blanchiment de capitaux. Il avait également contesté les chiffres relatifs aux recettes et aux dépenses de la commune présentés devant la Cour. Son co-prévenu, Mohamed Camara, n’a, quant à lui, pas encore été entendu sur le fond du dossier. À la prochaine audience, prévue le 9 décembre, l’Agent judiciaire de l’État (AJE) est attendu à la barre. L’interrogatoire d’Ahmed Sékou Traoré devrait également se poursuivre, sous réserve d’une reprise de la participation des avocats de l’État aux audiences.

items.title: DR Congo: Casi 6 de cada 10 mujeres y niñas adolescentes encuestadas denuncian un aumento de la violencia y los abusos en Ituri, provincia afectada por el ébola
items.description: Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo Source: UN Children's Fund KINSHASA/BUNIA/NUEVA YORK, 24 de noviembre de 2026 – Casi 6 de cada 10 mujeres y niñas adolescentes de 15 años o más encuestadas en Ituri, en la República Democrática del Congo, señalaron la aparición o el aumento de la violencia y los abusos en sus vidas desde que comenzó el brote de ébola. Los resultados, obtenidos a partir del primer estudio de seguimiento en tiempo real de la violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas durante el brote de una enfermedad contagiosa –realizado por UNICEF en colaboración con SOFEPADI, una organización dirigida por mujeres, y la Universidad de Washington en San Luis– revelan la manera en que el brote está afectando a la seguridad de las mujeres y las adolescentes en sus hogares y comunidades. “Las mujeres y las niñas se enfrentan a una creciente amenaza de violencia y abuso que se suma al brote de una enfermedad mortal y al conflicto que persiste en el este de la República Democrática del Congo”, afirmó Catherine Russell, Directora Ejecutiva de UNICEF. “Con demasiada frecuencia, en las zonas más afectadas no existen espacios de protección fuera del hogar a los que puedan acceder de forma segura”. Con base en 1.062 entrevistas con mujeres y adolescentes entre el 28 de agosto y el 15 de octubre, los resultados apuntan a la aparición o al aumento de al menos una forma de violencia o abuso. Más de una tercera parte de las encuestadas denunciaron un control cada vez mayor sobre los lugares adonde podían ir, su dinero y sus teléfonos, así como un aumento de los abusos emocionales y psicológicos y de la violencia física y sexual. Según los hallazgos, 7 de cada 10 encuestadas afirmaron que en su hogar se había aplicado al menos una medida de respuesta en materia de salud pública, como el aislamiento, la cuarentena o el rastreo de contactos. Entre quienes señalaron un aumento de la violencia y los abusos, 9 de cada 10 consideraron que el estrés y el miedo asociados al brote habían contribuido a dicho incremento. Casi la mitad de las mujeres y las adolescentes que intentaron acceder a servicios de atención y apoyo no pudieron hacerlo. Los trabajadores de primera línea informaron de que algunas mujeres y niñas limitaban sus desplazamientos para evitar contagiarse, mientras que en otros casos eran miembros de la familia u otras personas quienes las obligaban a quedarse encerradas en casa. Algunos de los establecimientos y servicios de los que antes dependían han cerrado o han sido destinados a otros fines. Las encuestadas también citaron la vergüenza, el miedo al agresor y la desconfianza. La demanda de los espacios seguros que permanecen abiertos y siguen siendo accesibles para las mujeres y las niñas afectadas por la violencia o en riesgo de sufrirla sigue aumentando. Por ejemplo, las visitas a ocho espacios seguros gestionados por SOFEPADI en Ituri aumentaron un 200%, al pasar de 1.183 entre enero y marzo a 3.548 entre julio y septiembre. En otra encuesta de UNICEF dirigida a unos 11.500 jóvenes de Ituri a través de U-Report, la plataforma digital de UNICEF para que los y las jóvenes compartan sus perspectivas sobre las cuestiones que les afectan, casi la mitad de las personas encuestadas afirmaron que el riesgo de sufrir violencia era mayor para las mujeres y las niñas desde que comenzó el brote. La violencia física y sexual fueron las preocupaciones más citadas. Las mujeres y las niñas corren más riesgo de contraer la enfermedad. El cuidado de familiares enfermos, la preparación del entierro de sus seres queridos y las frecuentes visitas a centros de salud (en muchos casos, para llevar a niños y niñas enfermos) también incrementan el riesgo de infección. Todo ello se suma a una situación que ya era frágil, después de años de conflicto y desplazamientos que habían expuesto a las mujeres y las niñas a niveles alarmantes de violencia de género mucho antes de que empezara el brote. Ahora, muchas denuncian aún más violencia en sus hogares y en sus comunidades. Desde que comenzó el brote, UNICEF y sus aliados han atendido a más de 3.300 supervivientes de violencia de género en Ituri y en Kivu del Norte y han brindado apoyo psicosocial y para la salud mental a casi 175.000 personas entre junio y octubre. Pero la protección de los niños y niñas y las mujeres, incluidos los servicios de atención a la violencia de género, sigue siendo uno de los ámbitos de respuesta con menor financiación, con un déficit del 76%. Los resultados del seguimiento se están poniendo a disposición de los coordinadores de la respuesta al ébola para que puedan fundamentar la toma de decisiones, mientras UNICEF mantiene su llamamiento a las autoridades gubernamentales, los aliados de respuesta y los donantes para garantizar los siguientes puntos: Hacer de la seguridad de las mujeres y las niñas un indicador fundamental de una respuesta eficaz al ébola. Trabajar con organizaciones locales de mujeres para detectar a tiempo los riesgos emergentes, actuar y evitar poner a las mujeres y las niñas en peligro o impedir que reciban ayuda. Asegurar que los servicios destinados a las mujeres y las niñas estén disponibles, sean accesibles y reciban financiación suficiente durante todo el brote, así como establecer nuevos servicios en las zonas más afectadas por el ébola. A medida que aumentan los riesgos y crece la demanda de apoyo, es fundamental que los servicios de atención a la violencia de género –incluidos los espacios seguros– tengan capacidad para responder. Incorporar el seguimiento de la violencia a la respuesta al actual brote de ébola y convertirlo en un componente de la preparación y la respuesta ante futuras emergencias de salud pública. Las organizaciones de mujeres deben formar parte oficialmente de los mecanismos de vigilancia, y deben establecerse salvaguardias que garanticen la confidencialidad y la seguridad. El seguimiento debe comenzar desde el inicio de cualquier brote. “No hay justificación para la violencia y los abusos contra mujeres y niñas”, afirmó Russell. “Su protección debe formar parte de la respuesta al ébola, y para ello debemos tener en cuenta sus experiencias. Eso incluye priorizar la prevención y los servicios destinados a las supervivientes”, aseguró Russell. Citas de aliados “Desde que comenzó el brote, cada vez más mujeres y niñas acuden a nuestros espacios seguros con la esperanza de ser escuchadas y recibir apoyo y protección, sin miedo ni estigma. Los espacios seguros deben permanecer abiertos y recibir los recursos necesarios durante toda la respuesta. El seguimiento y el apoyo deberían extenderse a otras zonas de riesgo”, dijo Sandrine Lusamba, Coordinadora Nacional de SOFEPADI. “Cuando las mujeres explican por qué la violencia ha comenzado o se ha agravado, muchas mencionan el miedo y la tensión que este brote ha llevado a sus hogares. Esas presiones pueden anticiparse. Si se mantiene el funcionamiento de los servicios existentes, se crean otros nuevos y se escucha a las mujeres a medida que se desarrolla la respuesta, se podrá evitar que esa presión se convierta en daño”, dijo la Dra. Lindsay Stark, Codirectora del Centro de Violencia y Salud de la Escuela de Salud Pública Bursky, Universidad de Washington en San Luis. #####

items.title: DR Congo: Gavi signe un accord avec le Serum Institute of India afin de garantir un accès rapide aux vaccins contre le virus Ebola Bundibugyo
items.description: Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo Source: GAVI Alliance L’engagement d’achat anticipé de Gavi garantit l’accès jusqu’à 1,5 million de doses de ChAdOx1 BDBV, un vaccin candidat contre le virus Ebola Bundibugyo développé conjointement par le Serum Institute of India et l’Oxford Vaccine Group de l’Université d’Oxford Cet accord est financé par le Fonds de première riposte de Gavi, l’approvisionnement restant subordonné aux résultats des essais cliniques, ainsi qu’à l’obtention par le vaccin candidat des autorisations réglementaires nécessaires et des recommandations politiques La Dre Sania Nishtar, directrice exécutive de Gavi : « Pour la deuxième urgence de santé publique de portée internationale depuis sa création, le Fonds de première riposte fonctionne comme prévu : il garantit un accès précoce et rapide aux vaccins, afin que les communautés puissent être protégées au plus vite. » Genève, le 24 novembre 2026 – Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin a annoncé aujourd’hui avoir signé un engagement d’achat anticipé avec le Serum Institute of India (SII) et Serum Life Sciences afin de garantir l’accès jusqu’à 1,5 million de doses de ChAdOx1 BDBV, un vaccin candidat contre la souche Bundibugyo du virus Ebola. Ces doses, financées par le Fonds de première riposte * de Gavi, pourraient être achetées si les essais cliniques donnaient des résultats concluants, si les autorisations réglementaires étaient obtenues et si des recommandations politiques appropriées étaient formulées en faveur de l’utilisation du vaccin. « Pour la deuxième urgence de santé publique de portée internationale depuis sa création, le Fonds de première riposte fonctionne comme prévu : il garantit un accès précoce et rapide aux vaccins, afin que les communautés puissent être protégées au plus vite », a déclaré la Dre Sania Nishtar, Directrice exécutive de Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin. « Alors que l’épidémie d’Ebola continue de ravager des communautés en République démocratique du Congo, nous devons agir de toute urgence pour veiller à ce que les procédures réglementaires soient en place, afin qu’il soit possible de mettre rapidement sur le marché ce vaccin candidat si les essais cliniques donnent des résultats positifs. C’est essentiel pour sauver des vies et garantir la sécurité de toutes et tous. » À ce jour, l’épidémie actuelle d’Ebola a engendré plus de 11 600 cas et causé plus de 5 700 décès, dont la grande majorité en République démocratique du Congo. Le ChAdOx1 BDBV est l’un des deux nouveaux vaccins candidats contre le virus Ebola Bundibugyo que l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS) a recommandés pour des essais cliniques dans le cadre de l’épidémie actuelle. Si, à l’issue des essais cliniques, le vaccin candidat obtient les autorisations réglementaires nécessaires et les recommandations du Groupe stratégique consultatif d’experts sur la vaccination de l’OMS, l’engagement d’achat anticipé de Gavi permettra de mettre rapidement ces doses à la disposition des populations touchées. Le SII a déjà produit la substance active nécessaire à la fabrication de plus d’un demi-million de doses du vaccin candidat afin d’en faciliter l’accès rapide. Adar Poonawalla, PDG du Serum Institute of India , a déclaré : « Une riposte efficace aux épidémies exige la capacité d’agir rapidement, la préparation et la collaboration mondiale jouant un rôle essentiel pour garantir un accès rapide aux vaccins. Grâce à notre accord avec Gavi, nous franchissons une étape importante pour veiller à ce que les stocks de vaccins puissent être mobilisés sans délai. En collaborant avec l’Oxford Vaccine Group et l’Université d’Oxford pour le développement du vaccin contre Ebola, nous nous engageons à garantir aux communautés touchées l’accès aux vaccins, renforçant ainsi la réponse mondiale aux épidémies causées par la souche Bundibugyo du virus Ebola. » L’annonce d’aujourd’hui s’inscrit dans le cadre du soutien global apporté par Gavi à la lutte contre l’épidémie actuelle d’Ebola . Jusqu’à 40 millions de dollars US provenant du mécanisme du Fonds de première riposte ont été alloués pour soutenir des accords visant à faciliter l’accès aux vaccins, tels que cet engagement d’achat anticipé. Le travail de Gavi en matière d’accès aux vaccins est mené en étroite collaboration avec la Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), ainsi qu’avec les Centres africains de contrôle et de prévention des maladies (Africa CDC), l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS), l’UNICEF et d’autres partenaires. Une enveloppe supplémentaire de 10 millions de dollars US provenant du Fonds de première riposte – dont 6 millions de dollars US ont déjà été engagés ou décaissés à la République démocratique du Congo, à l’Ouganda, aux Centres africains de contrôle et de prévention des maladies, à l’OMS et à l’UNICEF – contribue à préserver les services de vaccination systématique dans les communautés touchées et à protéger les agentes et agents de santé en première ligne. Ervebo, un vaccin contre le virus Ebola déjà existant et autorisé pour lutter contre la souche Zaïre du virus, est également utilisé dans le cadre de protocoles de recherche clinique. Gavi a débloqué un investissement supplémentaire de 7 millions de dollars US afin de fournir 70 000 doses du vaccin Ervebo déjà disponible, provenant de la réserve mondiale financée par Gavi. Ces doses sont actuellement administrées aux populations touchées en République démocratique du Congo dans le cadre des protocoles d’usage compassionnel d’urgence de l’OMS. Notes aux rédacteurs * Le Fonds de première riposte existe grâce aux gouvernements qui ont investi dans cet élément déterminant de la capacité de Gavi à faire face aux épidémies et aux pandémies. Gavi tient à saluer le soutien essentiel apporté par les États-Unis, le Japon, l’Italie, l’Allemagne, la Norvège et la France, dont les engagements ont permis d’assurer le financement intégral du Fonds de première riposte de Gavi, d’un montant de 500 millions de dollars US. Le Fonds de première riposte a également été mobilisé pour permettre une réponse rapide à l'urgence liée à la mpox en 2024. Pour en savoir plus, cliquez ici . À propos de Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin est un partenariat public-privé qui aide à vacciner plus de la moitié des enfants de la planète contre certaines des maladies les plus meurtrières. L’Alliance du Vaccin rassemble les gouvernements des pays donateurs et des pays bénéficiaires, l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé, l’UNICEF, la Banque mondiale, l’industrie du vaccin, les agences techniques, la société civile, la Fondation Gates ainsi que d’autres partenaires du secteur privé. Pour consulter la liste complète des gouvernements donateurs et des autres grandes organisations qui financent le travail de Gavi, veuillez cliquer ici . Depuis sa création en 2000, Gavi a aidé à vacciner une génération tout entière – soit plus de 1,3 milliard d'enfants – et à prévenir à terme plus de 23 millions de décès, ce qui a permis de réduire de moitié la mortalité infantile dans 78 pays à faible revenu. Gavi joue également un rôle essentiel dans l'amélioration de la sécurité sanitaire mondiale en soutenant les systèmes de santé et en finançant les stocks mondiaux de vaccins contre la maladie à virus Ebola, le choléra, la méningite, le mpox et la fièvre jaune. Après plus de deux décennies de progrès, Gavi s'attache désormais à protéger la nouvelle génération et surtout à atteindre les enfants zéro dose qui n'ont reçu aucune dose de vaccin. L'Alliance du Vaccin recourt à des mécanismes financiers innovants et aux technologies de pointe – allant de l'utilisation de drones à la biométrie – pour sauver des vies, prévenir les épidémies avant qu'elles ne se propagent et aider les pays à atteindre l'autosuffisance. En savoir plus sur www.gavi.org.fr et suivez-nous sur Bluesky , Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , TikTok , X et YouTube .

items.title: Conakry : la 12ᵉ édition du SBPME s’achève sur une note de satisfaction
items.description: Organisée du 20 au 23 novembre 2026 à Conakry, la 12ᵉ édition du Salon professionnel panafricain des banques, des institutions de microfinance, des fintechs, des assurances et des PME (SBPME) a tenu toutes ses promesses. Avec une vingtaine de pays représentés, plus d’une centaine d’exposants, plusieurs délégations internationales et des milliers de visiteurs, cette édition, placée sous la coordination de la Chambre de commerce, d’industrie et d’artisanat de Guinée (CCIAG), a été marquée par des échanges de haut niveau autour des enjeux liés au climat des affaires, des panels thématiques ainsi que des visites de stands. Lors de cette 12ᵉ édition, le SBPME a été une véritable plateforme de rencontres, de dialogue et de mise en relation entre les institutions financières et les acteurs économiques. Au-delà des échanges institutionnels, ce rendez-vous panafricain a mis en lumière les défis liés au financement des PME, à leur formalisation et à leur développement, tout en ouvrant des perspectives de coopération entre les différents acteurs du secteur privé africain. Le président du Fonds africain de garantie et de coopération économique (FAGACE), qui accompagne ce rendez-vous depuis sept ans, Ngueto Tiraïna Yambaye, a exprimé sa satisfaction quant à la réussite de cette manifestation, tout en saluant l’engagement des autorités guinéennes et des partenaires institutionnels. «Nous sommes particulièrement satisfaits de l’engagement des autorités guinéennes, du ministère du Commerce et de l’Industrie ainsi que de la Chambre de commerce pour la réussite de cette rencontre. Il est important de créer un cadre de dialogue entre les banques et les PME afin de renforcer leur confiance mutuelle et de faciliter le financement des activités économiques », a-t-il déclaré. Considérées comme des leviers essentiels pour faciliter l’accès au crédit, les mesures visant à renforcer les relations entre les institutions financières et les particuliers ont également été évoquées par Ngueto Tiraïna Yambaye, qui a rappelé les préalables nécessaires. «Concrètement, le Premier ministre a souhaité relever le taux de bancarisation de l'économie : tout Guinéen doit pouvoir disposer d'un compte bancaire, que ce soit dans une banque ou dans une institution de microfinance, afin que la circulation de l'argent liquide laisse davantage de place aux paiements monétiques. On utilise déjà le mobile banking, mais nous pouvons aller plus loin pour que chaque Guinéen ait le droit d'avoir un compte bancaire, car c'est à travers ce compte qu'il pourra accéder au crédit. C'est un cercle vertueux : si vous n'avez pas de compte bancaire, vous ne pouvez pas obtenir de crédit. Les banques doivent donc faire confiance au public et revoir également les frais de gestion des comptes», a-t-il expliqué. La représentante d’Atlantic Microfinance, Adama Yaya Diallo, a, dans sa communication, rappelé la vocation de son institution, qui porte principalement sur l’accompagnement des entreprises. «Nous sommes entrés en contact avec plusieurs PME qui exercent diverses activités que nous finançons. Nous leur avons donc proposé nos produits, pris leurs coordonnées et nous les invitons à venir dans nos locaux pour plus de précisions». Cette animatrice du réseau d’Atlantic Microfinance soutient qu’il n’y a pas d’obstacle en dehors de la formalisation. «Nous sommes dans un pays où les gens hésitent à se formaliser. Nous appelons les entrepreneurs à aller se formaliser. La formalisation ne coûte presque rien : en moins de 72 heures, vous pouvez obtenir votre RCCM, Ainsi, ils peuvent accéder au financement. L'argent est là, le financement est disponible, ils n'ont qu'à se formaliser et venir vers nous. À notre tour, nous ferons le maximum, le nécessaire, pour qu'ils aient accès au financement», a-t-elle expliqué. Prenant également part aux échanges, le président de la Confédération patronale unique des PME de Côte d’Ivoire, Dr Diomandé Moussa Elias Farakhan, est intervenu lors du panel consacré à la problématique du financement de l’agriculture et de l’élevage ainsi qu’à la structuration des chaînes de valeur. « Il y a plusieurs éléments qui entrent en ligne de compte dont le financement : il faut de l'argent pour financer une activité endogène, c'est-à-dire nos producteurs, ceux qui font des œufs et tout ça, ceux qui font l'élevage, qui font l'agriculture, qui font la pisciculture. Et pour nous, l'Afrique a déjà de l'argent parce que les financements endogènes, ils sont déjà récoltés. L'épargne, c'est plus de 4 000 milliards de dollars. Donc il faut qu'on trouve les mécanismes pour flécher ces financements vers les projets des petites et moyennes entreprises. Nous, nous croyons à la filiarisation. Il faut des filières, parce que ça permet de créer un écosystème, ça permet de créer un environnement où ceux qui vont suivre ce qu'on dit, ou ce qui va être mis en place, seront les meilleurs». Poursuivant son intervention, le Dr Diomandé Moussa Elias Farakhan a insisté sur l’orientation des financements vers les filières stratégiques et les filières de substances, ainsi que sur la possibilité de vendre à l’extérieur. «La vente à l'extérieur exige des critères. Il faut que les produits soient compétitifs et qand on dit « compétitivité », ça peut être le prix, ça peut être le produit, mais ça peut être également la qualité, la durabilité, le respect des normes. On ne peut pas fabriquer des produits dans des conditions d'hygiène déplorables. Il faut qu'il y ait une traçabilité. Donc, ce sont des éléments en termes d'industrialisation ; ce sont des petites choses qu'on peut régler facilement. Mais cela doit se faire dans un programme, dans un programme global. Et dans ce programme global qui traite la chaîne de valeur, on sait par exemple que si on est dans les œufs : on va faire un programme autour de la typologie des poules qui vont pondre ces œufs-là, en termes de productivité ; les installations et tout ça peuvent être évaluées. Et à partir de ce moment, on arrive à maîtriser cette chaîne de valeur avec tout l'écosystème, c'est-à-dire : les animaux, la nourriture, les vaccins, le personnel qui travaille là-dessus, et puis la vente». Très heureuse de prendre part à ce rendez-vous économique, la fondatrice et gérante de Binedou Global Service, une entreprise spécialisée dans la collecte et la transformation des déchets plastiques en pavés, briques et autres produits dérivés, Mariam Mohamed Keita, a présenté ses domaines d’expertise. « Nous ramassons les déchets abandonnés dans les caniveaux, dans les poubelles et dans les plages que nous ramassons pour vraiment trouver une solution à l'assainissement, à l'abandon des déchets plastiques dans les rues et à la promotion aussi de la gente féminine. Voilà, on s'est lancé dans tout ça pour trouver une solution à cette frustration qui est l'insalubrité à Conakry». Pour conclure, Mariam Mohamed Keita a souligné que ce cadre d’échange lui a permis de démystifier un sujet qui est resté longtemps un handicap pour bénéficier du crédit et booster son entreprise. «Ce salon, je dirais que ça m'a beaucoup apporté parce que là j'ai rencontré des personnes que je souhaitais vraiment rencontrer depuis des années on voulait rencontrer les PME et les banques pour leur expliquer les difficultés que nous rencontrons. Mais à travers ce salon ils sont venus vers nous, on les a posé directement les questions pour en savoir pourquoi souvent il y a des problèmes pour avoir des crédits, des financements pour nos activités. On a eu vraiment des réponses, ils nous ont répondu face à face, ce qui est parfois un peu difficile. Maintenant on sait où on doit aller et comment faire aussi» Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Conakry : la 12ᵉ édition du SBPME s’achève sur une note de satisfaction est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: The Surprising Pleasures of Aging Gracefully
items.description: “I hope I die before I get old,” a 21-year-old Roger Daltrey famously sneered on the Who’s 1965 single “My Generation.” At the time, the countercultural upshot was clear: Music was a young man’s game, especially rock and roll. Rock music embodied rebellion and fearlessness. It was about spitting in the face of elders who disapproved of what they could never understand. Who could trust a rock star still playing those kinds of songs well into middle age? Of course, the surviving members of the Who are now in their 80s and still performing, despite promises of retirement, because the benefits of playing decades-old songs to adoring crowds remain strong. The expectation of releasing new music has faded away. Audiences come to bask in memories from their youth or share their passions with their kids. The money is excellent. Classic rockers such as the Who, the Rolling Stones, and the Eagles set the template for hugely profitable late-in-life reunion tours; successive generations of bands have followed suit. Now the cycle continues with two defining British bands from the mid-’90s, who have reunited to remind the public that the music from the Britpop era was really just that good. Two new documentaries about Oasis and Pulp, inspired by their respective circa-2025 tours, capture the spirit of the bands while digging into how they’ve processed the passage of time—to fascinating effect. Oasis was the most successful of the Britpop groups; led by the brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, its swaggering rock music conveyed the maximalist melodrama of being young and in love with women, drugs, and ambition. Pulp was arguably the coolest Britpop group, whose front man, Jarvis Cocker, led with a sly, eccentric style and literary sensibility that stood in sharp contrast to his noisier peers. Like the Gallaghers, he seemed to genuinely relish his celebrity, but his relatively reserved personality made his indulgences seem chic and deliberate—potential grist for the lyrical mill, not simply rock-and-roll decadence. Don’t Look Back in Anger chronicles the highly anticipated Oasis reunion tour in 2025 that rejuvenated the band’s public image, following an acrimonious 2009 split. What Do You Do for an Encore? , for its part, combines a traditional concert film with a snapshot survey of Pulp’s lengthy career, and is narrated with wry humor by Cocker himself. Both documentaries attempt to bridge the gap between nostalgia for a past heyday and sanguine acceptance of a hazy future, while asking a simple yet difficult question: How do rock and rollers grow old without embarrassing themselves? In the ’90s, the British music media spent a lot of time publicizing an astroturfed competition between Oasis and its fellow chart-topper Blur , its baroque, Anglophilic-pop counterpart. Amid this sniping, Pulp stood apart as the round peg in a sea of square holes. A working-class kid from Sheffield, Cocker was 31 when Pulp’s best-known single, “Common People,” climbed the U.K. charts in 1995, making him something of an elder statesman relative to his musical peers. Draped in dapper outfits accentuating his lanky frame, Cocker represented an androgynous, cerebral alternative to the era’s boisterous masculinity. What Do You Do for an Encore? sketches out how Cocker graduated from a teenage outsider to a patron saint for sensitive, horny misfits. The documentary is anchored by performances from Pulp’s sold-out shows at London’s O2 Arena in June 2025 and is interspersed with “commercial breaks” during which Cocker, in voice-over, cheekily breaks the fourth wall to narrate his early childhood and experiences with fame. The film highlights Cocker’s alt-lothario stage presence as he sings about a world of hedonism and heartbreak, coming off as a veteran actor who’s only grown deeper into his role. In contrast, Don’t Look Back in Anger ’s directors, Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern, frequently cut away from Oasis’s performances to focus on the crowd itself, singling out individuals in tears or mid-embrace. They also incorporate numerous testimonials about how Oasis affected fans’ lives. Some are compact voice-over explanations about the power of friendship or self-confidence. Others are longer on-screen tributes, including one from a South Korean haenyeo (a female diver responsible for harvesting sea life) who explains how Oasis’s music gave her the strength to plunge into the water. Another features a survivor of the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing, who discusses how the song that gives the documentary its name helped her process survivor’s guilt. The film also goes to some lengths to imply that the Gallaghers’ reunion mended the culture at large, or at least provided the world with sufficient escapism and hope. Early in the film, Liam says, “When Oasis split up, things just went shit,” which is followed by a montage of news footage that includes the January 6 riots, Donald Trump dancing at a MAGA rally, and a food-delivery robot getting hit by a car. (No montage of positive world events following the tour is to be found.) Later, a Manchester priest speaks to a sparsely attended congregation about how crowds of Oasis fans resemble a pilgrimage and indicate a “shared longing for healing.” The message is clear: No matter what else has happened, the world is better with Oasis in it. Patience for this level of hyperbole obviously depends on the viewer’s affection for Oasis. As a longtime listener, I often found myself chafing against some of the overwrought fan reactions, despite their transparent sincerity. But I can attest to the accuracy of how the film portrays the public fervor that the Oasis reunion inspired in the U.K. In the days leading up to the Dublin show, my friends and I could not walk a few feet in the city without seeing an Oasis T-shirt or bucket hat. The show itself was pandemonium, with approximately 80,000 people singing along to every word of every song. I rarely attend concerts that are on this scale and get this level of hype, so at times I simply watched the crowd move in almost otherworldly unison. “I’d never come across an atmosphere like that at a concert before,” remarked Cocker, who attended one of Oasis’s Wembley shows. “It was like being at some kind of religious rally or something. It was amazing.” Oasis has been the subject of other documentaries, but my favorite is 2016’s Supersonic . The film is laser-focused on the Gallagher brothers’ conversational interplay, which, by default, makes it one of the funniest music documentaries ever released. Hearing Noel and Liam trade barbs about the other’s professional acumen or recount the same drug-fueled period in radically different terms, you might think that their real talent was giving hilarious interviews that exemplified their vulgar charisma. This time around, Noel and Liam—who have recently reconciled amidst years of estrangement—don’t exchange insults. Rather, the film chronicles their growing appreciation for each other as the tour transpires, which is expressed in hand-holding and hugs onstage. “It was all forgiven without saying a word,” Noel says of their beef, a notable reversal. They are older, softer men, who routinely express their gratitude for the opportunity to play 30-year-old songs to sold-out stadiums. This makes emotional sense for the Gallaghers and the film, but the scant display of their comedic chops is a little disappointing. Ironically, Don’t Look Back in Anger comes most alive whenever Noel and Liam speak semi-extemporaneously about each other. At one point, Noel expounds in voice-over about Liam’s aloof appeal before saying, as if he is remembering in real time, “I forgot how funny he was.” Cut to Liam, wearing enormous glasses, profanely explaining why he stands still onstage and then pondering whether Mick Jagger secretly wishes he didn’t have to do “‘Jumpin’ Jack Flash’ nonsense.” Noel cracking up at this rant in the background pulls more heartstrings than any onstage embrace. Pulp has also been the subject of a prior documentary: 2014’s A Film About Life, Death & Supermarkets , which depicts what was at the time billed as the group’s final U.K. show, in 2012, in Cocker’s hometown of Sheffield. Like Supersonic , this earlier film explains the appeal of Pulp better than the new one. Yet the 2026 documentary captures the emotions that come with unexpected longevity. In Supermarkets , for example, Cocker mentions wanting to provide Pulp with the tidy ending it didn’t get during its initial run. In Encore , however, he expresses the humility that comes with being unable to predict the future, now that his band has reunited. “You might be forgiven for thinking, after all these years, Why do we keep going? ” he narrates in his baritone. “I think the question you should really be asking yourself is this: Why wouldn’t we?” The Gallagher brothers arrive at a similar conclusion, as Liam expresses a quasi-mystical disbelief at the capacity of Oasis’s music to bring people together: “It’s bigger than me and Noel. It doesn’t belong to us.” Unlike Pulp, which is now on hiatus, Oasis will gear up for another worldwide tour next year, certainly to chase the hundreds of millions of dollars the band made in 2025, but also possibly to search for an answer to how and why, per Liam, “Oasis saves.” For my money, trying to determine the mass appeal of Oasis is like trying to understand why so many people like beer; you either get it or you don’t. But the choruses are really catchy. Despite some frustrations, watching Don’t Look Back in Anger and What Do You Do for an Encore? in quick succession proved strangely gratifying. I was aware that the filmmakers used my built-in affection for both of these bands to sell an image of them as wiser, more prudent men. Yet it is wise to appreciate your audience, and your remaining ability to galvanize them with your music. These films suggest that second or third acts are never guaranteed in life, especially in the realm of pop stardom. The Gallaghers and Cocker have composed many songs that are now old enough to drink and drive, and each carries power far beyond their initial impact. Performing onstage, these documentaries show, is a reminder that these older men are vessels for community and significance. At the same time, the hits don’t exist without them. The vessels themselves are worthy of celebration.
